course.title: Personal Finance and Investing
course.description: Judge which money choice costs more, and roughly how much, under Australian rules: tax, saving, borrowing, HECS-HELP, home loans, super, investing, insurance and scams.
course.audience: Adults and older students in Australia who earn or will earn income, and who want to judge offers and products themselves. They need percentages and nothing else. The course does not repeat the market theory in Economics or the expected value and utility in Decision Theory.

paragraphs: Judge which money choice costs more, and roughly how much, under Australian rules: tax, saving, borrowing, HECS-HELP, home loans, super, investing, insurance and scams.
outcomes: You'll be able to read an ATO tax table for a stated year and say how much of an extra dollar you keep.
You'll be able to size an emergency fund in months of spending and decide where to hold it.
You'll be able to judge, from rate, time and fees, which of two credit, loan or fund choices costs more and roughly by how much.
You'll be able to tell the true cost of an 'interest-free' or buy now pay later offer from its conditions.
You'll be able to explain how super contributions, caps, fees and access work, and test a contribution against the cap.
You'll be able to match an investment mix to a goal's time frame and say what diversification does and does not remove.

modules.title: Pay and saving
modules.description: From gross pay to take-home, a budget with an emergency fund, and how time and rates grow a balance.

modules.title: Borrowing
modules.description: What cards, interest-free offers, HECS-HELP and a home loan cost, and what an offset account is worth.

modules.title: Superannuation
modules.description: The guarantee, contributions and caps, access, and what fees and fund choice do over a working life.

modules.title: Investing
modules.description: Risk, return and time; diversification, index funds and ETFs; property against shares.

modules.title: Protecting what you have
modules.description: Insurance that matches real risks, and the patterns of scams.

concepts.title: Tax band
concepts.summary: Each rate applies only to the income that falls inside its band, as in '30c for each $1 over $45,000'.

concepts.title: Marginal rate
concepts.summary: The rate on the next dollar earned. It decides how much of a raise or an extra shift is kept.

concepts.title: Average rate
concepts.summary: Total tax divided by taxable income. It is lower than the marginal rate once income passes the first bands.

concepts.title: Medicare levy
concepts.summary: 2% of taxable income, charged on top of the table. The ATO's rates do not include it.

concepts.title: Income year
concepts.summary: Rates belong to a stated financial year: the first band was 16c in 2025-26 and is 15c in 2026-27.

concepts.title: Budget
concepts.summary: A list of the money coming in and the money going out, checked against bank statements and reviewed monthly.

concepts.title: Irregular costs
concepts.summary: Annual bills and surprises such as car registration or a vet bill. They break a budget that lists only monthly bills.

concepts.title: Surplus
concepts.summary: What is left when expenses are taken from income. It is where saving comes from.

concepts.title: Emergency fund
concepts.summary: Money kept for urgent, unexpected costs. A good target is three months of expenses.

concepts.title: Where to keep it
concepts.summary: A separate account, or an offset account on a home loan, so that it is easy to reach and hard to spend by accident.

concepts.title: Compound interest
concepts.summary: Interest earned on the principal and on interest already added.

concepts.title: Simple interest
concepts.summary: Interest on the starting amount only.

concepts.title: Rule of 72
concepts.summary: Years to double is roughly 72 divided by the yearly rate in per cent.

concepts.title: Inflation and CPI
concepts.summary: The rate at which the prices of what households buy rise; the CPI measures it on a basket of goods and services.

concepts.title: Keeping up with prices
concepts.summary: A rate below the inflation rate leaves a balance that buys less; HELP indexation keeps a debt in line with prices.

concepts.title: Purchase rate
concepts.summary: The yearly interest rate on purchases once any interest-free period has not applied. The average is over 18%.

concepts.title: Interest-free days
concepts.summary: Days with no interest on purchases, which apply only if the full balance is paid by the due date.

concepts.title: Card fees
concepts.summary: Annual or monthly fee, rewards program fee, late fee, cash advance fee, overseas fee.

concepts.title: Credit risk
concepts.summary: The bank's view of the chance of not being repaid, which the RBA says lifts card rates above home-loan rates.

concepts.title: Balance transfer
concepts.summary: Moving a debt to a card or loan with a low or 0% introductory rate; it saves money only if repaid in that period.

concepts.title: Buy now pay later
concepts.summary: Paying by instalments, usually without interest and with fees instead.

concepts.title: BNPL fees
concepts.summary: Late fees, monthly account-keeping fees, payment processing fees and establishment fees; bank overdrawn fees can follow.

concepts.title: Interest-free deal
concepts.summary: Goods paid for in stages over a fixed time, often 12, 24 or 60 months, with no interest charged during it. The deal usually runs through a store card or a credit card, and the retailer is not the lender.

concepts.title: The minimum-repayment trap
concepts.summary: Minimum repayments will not clear the balance by the end date, and interest, up to 29%, can then be charged on what is left.

concepts.title: Credit file effects
concepts.summary: Applications trigger credit checks and late or missed payments can be reported.

concepts.title: HELP debt
concepts.summary: A study loan repaid through the tax system. It is not charged interest but is indexed.

concepts.title: Repayment income
concepts.summary: Taxable income plus reportable fringe benefits, net investment losses, reportable super contributions and exempt foreign income.

concepts.title: Marginal repayment
concepts.summary: From 2025-26 the compulsory repayment is worked out only on the income above each threshold (2026-27: nil to $69,528, then 15c per $1, then 17c per $1 above $129,717).

concepts.title: Indexation
concepts.summary: Applied on 1 June to the part of the debt older than 11 months, at the lower of CPI and WPI growth. Like interest, it makes the debt grow.

concepts.title: Voluntary repayment
concepts.summary: A repayment made before 1 June (at least 5 business days) accrues less indexation.

concepts.title: Principal and interest
concepts.summary: A loan whose repayments cover interest and pay down the amount borrowed. Interest-only loans do not reduce the debt during the interest-only period.

concepts.title: Loan term
concepts.summary: A shorter term means higher repayments and less interest; a longer term means lower repayments and more interest.

concepts.title: Key Facts Sheet
concepts.summary: A compulsory, same-layout summary: interest rate, personalised comparison rate, total to be paid back, monthly repayment and fees.

concepts.title: Offset account
concepts.summary: A transaction account linked to the loan; its balance is taken off the loan balance before interest is worked out each day.

concepts.title: Stress test
concepts.summary: Working out repayments as if rates were 3% higher.

concepts.title: Super guarantee
concepts.summary: The minimum employer contribution: 12% from 1 July 2025, paid on top of wages; from 1 July 2026 it is worked out on qualifying earnings.

concepts.title: Concessional contributions
concepts.summary: Before-tax contributions: employer contributions, salary sacrifice, and personal contributions claimed as a deduction. Capped at $32,500 in 2026-27 across all funds, and taxed at 15% in the fund.

concepts.title: Non-concessional contributions
concepts.summary: After-tax contributions, capped at $130,000 in 2026-27.

concepts.title: Preservation and conditions of release
concepts.summary: Super is preserved until a condition is met: turning 65, or reaching preservation age (55 to 60 by birth date; 60 from 1 July 1964) and retiring.

concepts.title: Illegal early access
concepts.summary: Schemes that release super for credit card debt, a car or a holiday are illegal; the amount is taxed as income and penalties apply.

concepts.title: MySuper
concepts.summary: The default product: simple, low-cost, few standardised fees and one balanced option.

concepts.title: Like for like
concepts.summary: Comparing the same type of option over the same period, for example two balanced options over five years.

concepts.title: Stapled fund
concepts.summary: The existing fund an employer finds through the ATO when a new employee chooses none.

concepts.title: Duplicate accounts
concepts.summary: Several accounts can charge duplicate fees and insurance premiums, but consolidating can lose insurance.

concepts.title: Asset classes
concepts.summary: Shares, fixed income including bonds, property and cash.

concepts.title: Defensive and growth
concepts.summary: Defensive assets aim to protect money and have lower long-term returns; growth assets aim to rise over the long term and can fall in value.

concepts.title: Risk
concepts.summary: The chance and size of losses; more return potential usually comes with more risk, which does not guarantee a higher return.

concepts.title: Time frame
concepts.summary: Cash is often used for goals within 3 years; shares and property generally suit goals at least 5 years away. These are guides, not guarantees.

concepts.title: Diversified mixes
concepts.summary: Growth options hold about 85% growth assets, balanced about 70%, conservative about 30%.

concepts.title: Diversification
concepts.summary: Spreading money so that no one asset or risk dominates.

concepts.title: Diversifiable and market risk
concepts.summary: The fall of one company can be diversified away; the fall of the whole market cannot be removed by holding more shares.

concepts.title: Index fund
concepts.summary: A fund that aims to replicate an index's performance, before fees and expenses, without picking stocks.

concepts.title: ETF
concepts.summary: A managed fund bought and sold on an exchange. A sector ETF holds one slice of the market.

concepts.title: Drift and rebalancing
concepts.summary: As shares rise against bonds, a mix drifts towards more risk; rebalancing moves it back.

concepts.title: Cash-flow shortfall
concepts.summary: Rent less loan repayments and costs. Simon and Tiana's is $1,416 a month.

concepts.title: Entry, exit and ongoing costs
concepts.summary: Stamp duty, legal and agent's fees at purchase and sale; body corporate, management and repairs while owning.

concepts.title: Gearing
concepts.summary: Borrowing to invest, which magnifies both gains and losses, and the loan must be repaid whatever the investment does.

concepts.title: Margin call
concepts.summary: A demand to cut a loan back when its ratio to the investment's value passes the lender's limit (usually 70%).

concepts.title: Concentration
concepts.summary: One asset in one place carries the risk of that place.

concepts.title: Income protection
concepts.summary: Pays a share of your pay before tax, often 75% or 90%, while illness or injury stops you working. The waiting period (14 days to two years) and the benefit period (two or five years, or to a set age) decide how much is paid.

concepts.title: Life cover
concepts.summary: A lump sum on death, which matters when others depend on your income or you carry large debts; the amount is what is needed minus what would be received.

concepts.title: Insurance through super
concepts.summary: Default cover is paid for out of the balance, which reduces retirement savings.

concepts.title: Health cover
concepts.summary: Ambulance, hospital and extras. Premiums are community rated and waiting periods apply.

concepts.title: Medicare levy surcharge
concepts.summary: 0%, 1%, 1.25% or 1.5% of income for MLS purposes, on the whole income, for those over the threshold without an appropriate level of hospital cover.

concepts.title: Investment scam
concepts.summary: A fake product offered by someone who is not who they claim to be; the product does not exist.

concepts.title: Red flags
concepts.summary: Guaranteed or very high returns, pressure to decide, no AFS licence, unregistered prospectus, payment by gift card or cryptocurrency.

concepts.title: Trust-building
concepts.summary: Scripted calls, fake platforms and small early 'profits' that make a larger payment feel safe.

concepts.title: Reports against losses
concepts.summary: The most-reported contact method is not necessarily the costliest; the median and total loss differ by method.

concepts.title: Stop, Check, Protect
concepts.summary: Do not pay or give details when unsure; check who you are dealing with; act quickly if something feels wrong.

lessons.title: From gross pay to take-home

lead.text: Here is the ATO's table of tax rates for the 2026-27 income year, for people who were Australian residents for tax purposes for the full year and who have the full tax-free threshold. Each row is a **tax band**, a stretch of taxable income with a rule of its own, and the rule for the second band says 15c for each $1 over $18,200. A person with a taxable income of $44,000 has $25,800 above that line, so their tax is 15c on each of those dollars, which is $3,870.

The third row looks different, because it reads $4,020 plus 30c on each dollar over $45,000. The $4,020 is not an extra charge. It is the tax on the first $45,000, which is 15c on the $26,800 between $18,200 and $45,000, written out so that you can start from there. Only the dollars above $45,000 pay 30c, and the same pattern repeats in the later rows.

afterFigure.text: Whichever row an income lands in, **a rate applies only to the dollars above the line where its band starts**, and the dollars below keep the rates of their own bands.

reveal.text: Crossing a line changes the rate on the dollars above it and leaves the dollars below it alone.

lead.text: What does Priya's raise cost her? It is easy to price once you split it at the line. The first $1,000 takes her income from $44,000 to $45,000, where the rate is still 15c, so it adds $150 of tax. The second $1,000 sits above $45,000, where the rate is 30c, so it adds $300. Her $2,000 raise adds $450 of tax, and she keeps $1,550 of it before the second charge that comes on top, which we meet shortly.

The rate on the next dollar has a name, the **marginal rate**. Priya's was 15c at $44,000 and became 30c once she passed $45,000. It is the rate that answers questions such as whether an extra shift is worth taking or how much of a bonus you will keep, because those questions are about dollars you have not earned yet.

There is a second rate, and it is easy to mistake for the first. Take a taxable income of $100,000. The tax is $4,020 plus 30c on the $55,000 above $45,000, which is $4,020 plus $16,500, or $20,520, and $20,520 divided by $100,000 is about 20.5%. We call that the **average rate**: the whole tax bill as a share of the whole income.

At the same income the marginal rate is 30c, because the next dollar lies in the 30c band. The two differ because the first $18,200 pays nothing and the next $26,800 pays only 15c, and those cheaper dollars pull the average down.

afterFigure.text: In the figure the curve is the tax bill at each income. Its steepness at your income is the marginal rate, and it steepens at each line where a band begins, while the dashed line from the origin has the steepness of your average rate. At $135,000 the bill is $31,020, about 23% of the income, yet the next dollar is already taxed at 37c.

diagram.caption: Use the buttons to move the marker. The thick part of the line is the band the next dollar falls in, and the dashed line from the origin has the slope of the average rate.

lead.text: Under the ATO's table there is a short note saying the Medicare levy of 2% is not part of those rates. The levy is 2% of taxable income and is charged on top, so every extra dollar of income costs the rate of its band plus 2c. At $100,000 the next dollar costs 30c plus 2c, which is 32c, and the person keeps 68c of it.

The levy adds to the whole bill too. At $100,000 it is 2% of $100,000, or $2,000, so tax and levy together come to $22,520, about 22.5% of the income. Whenever a question asks how much you keep or how much you pay, check whether it means the table alone or the table plus the levy.

steps.headline: How much of a $5,000 raise does Sam keep when his taxable income is $80,000?

lead.text: The method is to find the band the raise lands in, add the 2c of levy to its rate, and take that share of the raise.

workedSteps.text: Find the band. Sam's income rises from $80,000 to $85,000, and both sit in the $45,001 to $135,000 band, so the whole raise is taxed at 30c.
Add the Medicare levy, which is charged on every extra dollar of taxable income as well.
Take that share of the raise.
Subtract it from the raise to see what Sam keeps.

steps.headline: How much of a $10,000 raise does Lena keep when her taxable income goes from $40,000 to $50,000?

lead.text: Lena's raise crosses the $45,000 line, so it has two parts. Two of the lines are left for you.

workedSteps.text: Split the raise where the rate changes. The first $5,000 takes her from $40,000 to $45,000, inside the 15c band, and the second $5,000 takes her from $45,000 to $50,000, inside the 30c band.
Add the levy to the first part and find what each of its dollars costs.
The second part costs 30c plus 2c, which is 32c a dollar. Together the two parts cost:
Take the total from the raise to find what Lena keeps.

reveal.text: The 23% describes the whole income. Overtime is priced at the rate of the highest band reached, plus the levy.

lead.text: Every rate in this lesson belongs to a financial year, and the ATO publishes a table for each. The 2025-26 table taxed the first band at 16c on each $1 over $18,200, and the 2026-27 table taxes it at 15c. The fixed amounts in the later rows move with it, so the third band was $4,288 plus 30c in 2025-26 and is $4,020 plus 30c now.

A worker on $40,000 paid 16c on $21,800, which is $3,488, in 2025-26, and pays 15c on the same $21,800, which is $3,270, in 2026-27. Anyone above $45,000 pays $268 less than before, since the 1c cut applies to the same $26,800 of income. A budget built on last year's table is therefore out by $218 at $40,000 and by $268 above $45,000, and a figure with no year attached can't be trusted.

afterFigure.text: Two other limits are worth knowing. The table is for residents for the full year with the full tax-free threshold, and it leaves out the Medicare levy and the Medicare levy surcharge, an extra charge of up to 1.5% for some higher earners without private health insurance. A real bill also depends on things the table does not cover: deductions and tax offsets, which this course does not teach, and HELP repayments, which have a lesson of their own.

diagram.alt: Two versions of the ATO table, 2026-27 and 2025-26. The rates match except in the first taxed band, 15c against 16c, and the tax at the top of each band is $268 lower in 2026-27. A third view compares the tax on $40,000: $3,488 in 2025-26 and $3,270 in 2026-27.

reveal.text: A rate belongs to one income year. When a source gives a figure with no year, find out which table it used.

lessons.orientation: Read an Australian income tax table for a stated year and say how much of an extra dollar of pay is kept, why that differs from the average rate, and what the 2% Medicare levy adds.
lessons.nextAction: Build a monthly budget from take-home pay, then size an emergency fund in months of spending.

blocks.text: Imagine a tax table with one rule: nothing is taxed up to $20,000, and income over $20,000 is taxed at 10c for each $1 over. The table is invented, but the wording is the wording of real ones. Zoe's taxable income is $30,000, and the question is what she owes.

The words 'for each $1 over' carry the whole rule, and reading them correctly decides how much of a raise, a bonus or an extra shift you keep. It also settles whether a friend is right to warn you that a raise will push you into a higher tax bracket and leave you worse off.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read a 2026-27 tax table, say how much of a raise you keep, and explain why that differs from your average rate.
intro.whyItMatters: A budget built on the wrong rate or the wrong year can be out by hundreds of dollars, and a raise is easier to judge once you know what happens to the next dollar.

recap.keyIdea: Each rate in the table applies only to the dollars above its line, so the rate on your next dollar, plus 2c for the Medicare levy, shows how much of a raise you keep, and it differs from your average rate.

blocks.text: You read the 2026-27 table band by band, split Priya's raise at $45,000 and priced each part, and saw that a [[marginal rate|The rate on the next dollar earned. Met in 'From gross pay to take-home'.]] of 30c at $100,000 sits beside an [[average rate|The whole tax bill divided by the whole income. Met in 'From gross pay to take-home'.]] of about 20.5%. The 2% Medicare levy comes on top of the table, so the next dollar costs 2c more than its band says, and the 2025-26 table shows why every rate needs its year.

recap.nextHook: Next we start from take-home pay, build a monthly budget and decide how much to hold back for emergencies.

lessons.title: Budgets and emergency funds

lead.text: A **budget** lists the money coming in and the money going out for a month, so that you can see what is left. Moneysmart's guide starts with income, which means wages, government payments and investment income, and it says to work out an average if your income changes from week to week. It then sorts spending into three groups, and the figure sets an invented household's month out that way.

Essentials are the regular costs you cannot easily skip: rent or a mortgage, groceries, power, gas and phone bills, medical costs, insurance and transport. Debt repayments are what you pay each month on a personal loan or a credit card. The third group holds the costs that do not arrive evenly, such as car servicing and repairs, annual bills and pet costs. To make sure nothing is missing, Moneysmart suggests checking the list against your bank statements and noting what each expense is for, how much it is and when you pay it.

afterFigure.text: In the figure the three groups add up to $4,660 against an income of $5,200. The third group has the smallest total, and it is the group most likely to be left off a list.

lead.text: The third group is easy to forget because it does not turn up every month. A yearly bill of $1,200 is the same as $100 a month, but it is paid on one day, and a household that has not set the $100 aside will have to find $1,200 at once. The usual answer is to treat these as **irregular costs** and give each one a monthly share in the budget, even though the bill itself is paid on another schedule.

In the figure the household's regular lines leave $790 a month. Its irregular costs come to $3,000 a year, which is $250 a month, and once they are counted the **surplus**, what is left when expenses are taken from income, falls to $540. The surplus is where saving comes from. A household that spends more than it earns has a shortfall instead, and Moneysmart says to look for ways to spend less.

afterFigure.text: A budget also has to keep up with the household. Moneysmart suggests checking it each month and updating it when income changes, when bills go up or when goals change.

reveal.text: The same savings last longer against smaller spending, so the size of a safety net is a number of months.

lead.text: Moneysmart describes an **emergency fund** as money you save for urgent or unexpected costs, so that you do not have to borrow when something happens. Its suggested target is three months of expenses. To find your own, take the monthly expenses from your budget and multiply them by the number of months you want to cover.

That is why the two households above are not equally safe. A's $9,000 covers three months of its spending and B's covers two, so a fund is best described as **months of cover** and not as a sum of dollars. B would need $13,500 to match A's three months. If you can only save a little, Moneysmart's advice is to start anyway: $20 a week comes to over $1,000 in a year.

afterFigure.text: Moneysmart adds that a longer view justifies a bit more, for example if you might be unable to work for a while, and that income protection insurance, which a later lesson covers, is another way to prepare for that.

steps.headline: How big should an emergency fund be for the household in the figure, if it wants three months of cover?

lead.text: The method is to find the monthly expenses, multiply by the months of cover, and compare the result with the surplus.

workedSteps.text: Take the monthly expenses from the budget. The three groups, with the irregular costs as monthly shares, come to $4,660.
Multiply by the months of cover. Three months is Moneysmart's suggested target.
Compare the target with the surplus of $540 a month to see how long saving would take.
Read the result as a plan. A first goal of one month's spending would take about nine months of saving.

steps.headline: How big a fund does a household need for three months of cover when it takes home $4,000 a month and spends $2,800?

lead.text: This invented household is simpler than the first one. Two of the lines are left for you.

workedSteps.text: Decide which monthly figure to multiply. The household takes home $4,000 and spends $2,800 a month.
Multiply the spending by the months of cover.
Find how fast the fund can grow. The surplus is what is left each month.
Divide the target by the surplus to see how long saving would take.

lead.text: A fund has one job. Moneysmart says to keep the fund for costs that must be paid quickly at a time when you have no other money for them, and to save up for a few weeks if the cost can wait. Its example is Eva, who set up an automatic transfer of $10 from her wage every payday. After two years of saving, her car broke down, and she paid for the $1,000 repair from the fund without using a credit card or asking her family for help.

So the test is whether a cost is urgent and unplanned. A failed car that someone needs to get to work this week passes it. A holiday sale with a deadline does not, because a bargain is an opportunity and can be saved for, and neither does an annual bill that falls due every year, because that belongs in the budget as an irregular cost. A deposit on a home is a savings goal of its own.

reveal.text: Urgent and unplanned is the test. A want can wait, and a yearly bill is known in advance.

lead.text: Where should the fund live? Moneysmart suggests a separate, high-interest savings account, which makes it harder to spend the money by accident on everyday things. It also suggests automating the saving with a transfer from the account your wage lands in, and adding extra money such as a tax refund when you can. The same idea works for the whole budget: separate accounts for bills, for spending and for savings, with transfers set up on pay day, keep the plan running without a decision every month.

A household with a home loan has a second choice, an **offset account**. It is linked to the loan, and the money in it lowers the loan balance that interest is charged on, while you can still reach the money quickly. A later lesson looks at how much that saves. What the offset does is cut the interest you are charged, and it does not pay interest to you.

reveal.text: The offset gives the fund a second job, cutting loan interest, without locking the money away.

lessons.orientation: Sort a month of household spending into essentials, debt repayments and irregular costs, say whether it leaves a surplus, and size and place an emergency fund in months of spending.
lessons.nextAction: See how a balance compounds over time and how inflation changes what it can buy.

blocks.text: A household adds up its monthly bills, compares them with its income and finds $500 left over each month. That sounds comfortable, until you remember what a list of monthly bills leaves out: the car service that falls due once a year, the annual bills that arrive in a single month, and the vet visit nobody planned.
A list of the money coming in and the money going out is only as useful as its lines. Choosing them well also tells you how much to keep aside for the costs that cannot be planned.

intro.promise: By the end you'll sort a month of spending into groups, say what surplus it leaves, and size an emergency fund in months of spending.
intro.whyItMatters: A fund measured in months shows how long you could manage without borrowing, and a budget with every group in it shows how much you can really save.

recap.keyIdea: A budget sorts spending into essentials, debt repayments and irregular costs, the surplus decides what can be saved, and an emergency fund is sized in months of spending, with three months a common target.

blocks.text: You sorted a month of spending into three groups, turned $3,000 of yearly costs into $250 a month and watched the [[surplus|What is left when expenses are taken from income. Met in 'Budgets and emergency funds'.]] fall from $790 to $540. A fund is measured in months of spending, so the same $9,000 covers three months for one household and two for another, and it is kept for costs that are urgent and unplanned, in a separate account or in an offset account.

recap.nextHook: Next we look at how a balance grows over time, and how rising prices can undo some of that growth.

lessons.title: Compounding, inflation and time

lead.text: Mira's balance after one year is $1,050, and the second year's interest is 5% of $1,050, which is $52.50, so after two years she has $1,102.50. The extra $2.50 is interest earned on interest. Interest that is paid on the original amount and also on the interest already added is **compound interest**. If it were paid only on the original amount, it would be **simple interest**, and Mira would earn $50 in every year.

The difference looks tiny in year two, $2.50 on $1,000, but it is not a one-off. Every year the balance is bigger than it was the year before, so every year's interest is bigger too, and the gap between the two kinds widens. The same rule works against you on a debt that is left to grow.

Moneysmart works through $10,000 at 3% a year with interest added every month. After 5 years the balance is $11,616, after 10 years $13,494 and after 20 years $18,208. Subtract each balance from the one before and you find what each stretch earned: $1,616 in the first five years, $1,878 in the next five and $4,714 in the last ten.

The rate never changed, yet the second five years earned $262 more than the first. The reason is the balance. In years 6 to 10 the interest was worked out on balances from about $11,600 to $13,500, and in years 1 to 5 on balances from $10,000 to $11,600.

afterFigure.text: Averaged by year, the first stretch earned about $323 a year, the second about $376 and the last about $471, so each year of the last ten earned almost half as much again as each of the first five. Moneysmart's own advice follows from this: start early.

reveal.text: The balance is what interest feeds on, so a longer time helps mainly by making the balance bigger.

lead.text: Now put the two kinds of interest side by side on $10,000 at 5% a year for twenty years. With simple interest the balance climbs by the same $500 every year, a straight line to $20,000. With compound interest, here with the interest added every month, each stretch starts from a bigger balance than the one before, so the line bends upward and ends near $27,126.

The gap is small early on and large later. After 10 years the compound balance is about $16,470 against $15,000, a gap of $1,470, and after 20 years it is $27,126 against $20,000, a gap of $7,126. Moneysmart notes that some term deposits use simple interest, so it is worth asking which kind an account uses.

afterFigure.text: The same rule works against a borrower. Unpaid interest on a debt is added to what is owed, and the next interest is worked out on the larger amount.

reveal.text: Adding interest to the balance is what turns a straight line into a curve.

lead.text: How long does money take to double? In 1494 Luca Pacioli's *Summa de arithmetica* gave a rule of thumb, which we call the **Rule of 72**: divide 72 by the yearly interest rate in per cent, and the answer is roughly the number of years to double with compound interest. At 6% that is 72 ÷ 6, or 12 years, and the exact figure is 11.9 years. At 3% the rule gives 24 years against an exact 23.4, and at 9% it gives 8 against 8.04.

The rule is an estimate, and its use is that you can do it in your head. It also exposes a common slip. Dividing 100 by the rate gives 16.7 years at 6%, and that is the doubling time for simple interest, where each year adds only 6% of the original amount. Compounding doubles money sooner because the interest earns interest. You can check the rule against Moneysmart's balances: at 3% it says 24 years to double, and after 20 years the balance of $18,208 has reached about 1.8 times the start, on its way there.

steps.headline: About how long will money take to grow to four times its size at 6% a year?

lead.text: The method is to find the doubling time with the Rule of 72 and then count how many doublings the target needs.

workedSteps.text: Find the doubling time. Divide 72 by the yearly rate in per cent.
Count the doublings. Four times the start is double, then double again.
Multiply the doubling time by the number of doublings.
Check the size of the answer. The exact figure at 6% is about 23.8 years, so the rule is close.

reveal.text: The rule turns a rate into a doubling time in one division. Simple interest would be slower.

lead.text: Interest tells you how a balance grows in dollars, and prices tell you what those dollars buy. The RBA describes **inflation** as a rise in the general level of prices for what households buy, and it measures it by how fast those prices change. The best-known measure is the Consumer Price Index, or **CPI**: the Australian Bureau of Statistics prices a basket of goods and services that households buy, and the CPI reports how much the cost of that basket has changed, as a percentage.

Suppose, with made-up figures, an account pays 3% a year while prices rise 4%. After a year $100 has become $103, but the basket that cost $100 now costs $104. The balance is 3% bigger and it buys about 1% less than it did a year earlier. Moneysmart makes the same point about cash: it has a very low risk of losing money, but rising prices may reduce what it can buy.

reveal.text: A balance can grow in dollars and still fall in what it buys, when prices grow faster.

lead.text: A balance keeps up with prices when its growth rate is at least the inflation rate, and it falls behind when the rate is lower. The shortfall is small in a single year and adds up over many, which is why cash held for a long time can lose buying power even though it never loses a dollar.

A debt can be set up to keep pace on purpose. The ATO describes indexation of a study and training loan as adjusting the loan in line with the CPI or the Wage Price Index, whichever is lower, so that its real value is kept. A later lesson on HECS-HELP looks at how that indexation works, and it behaves much like interest on the debt.

reveal.text: Indexation moves a debt with prices, so the debt keeps its real value while the number of dollars owed grows.

lessons.orientation: Judge from a rate, a time and a starting amount how fast a balance grows, use the Rule of 72 to estimate doubling, and say when a rate fails to keep up with prices.
lessons.nextAction: Look at what a credit card costs for different ways of using it.

blocks.text: Mira puts $1,000 into an account that pays 5% a year, and the interest is added to her balance at the end of each year. After the first year she has earned $50. In the second year the account pays 5% again, and the question is what that 5% is worked out on.

The answer decides whether a balance grows by the same dollars every year or by more each year as it gets bigger. The second kind describes savings where the interest stays in the account and debts where it is left unpaid, and it makes time as important as the rate.

intro.promise: By the end you'll judge how fast a balance grows from its rate and time, estimate doubling with the Rule of 72, and say when a rate fails to keep up with prices.
intro.whyItMatters: A rate quoted without a time, or a savings rate compared with nothing, tells you little, because time and prices change what the same rate is worth.

recap.keyIdea: Compound interest earns interest on interest, so each year's dollars grow with the balance, the Rule of 72 estimates doubling time, and a rate lower than inflation leaves a balance that buys less.

blocks.text: You saw $10,000 at 3% earn $1,616 in five years and $1,878 in the next five, because later interest is worked out on a bigger balance, and you used the [[Rule of 72|Divide 72 by the yearly rate in per cent to estimate the years money takes to double. Met in 'Compounding, inflation and time'.]] to estimate doubling at 4% and 6%. Against that, a balance keeps up with [[inflation|A rise in the prices of what households buy, measured by the CPI. Met in 'Compounding, inflation and time'.]] only if its rate is at least the rate at which prices rise.

recap.nextHook: Next we turn from saving to borrowing and ask what a credit card costs for different ways of using it.

lessons.title: Credit cards

lead.text: A credit card can cost money in several ways at once. The **purchase rate** is the yearly interest rate charged on what you buy when the card's interest-free period does not apply. Moneysmart says the average is over 18% and that rates can differ by more than 10 percentage points between cards. On top of the rate there is an annual or monthly fee, a fee for the rewards program if the card has one, and other fees, such as a late repayment fee, a cash advance fee, a fee for going over the credit limit and a fee for using the card overseas.

Moneysmart adds that complimentary extras such as travel insurance are usually not free, since their cost can be covered by higher interest or fees. So what a card costs depends on how the holder uses it, and the rest of the lesson follows two kinds of holder, one who pays in full and one who carries a balance.

Why would a card charge over 18% when a home loan costs far less? The RBA's explanation is about risk. For every loan a bank makes, it assesses the chance that the borrower will not repay, which is called **credit risk**, and that assessment helps set the interest rate. A bank that expects to lose money more often on cards than on home loans will charge more on cards, and the RBA adds that a bank's view of these risks can change over time.
At 18% a balance is expensive to keep, so how you use the card, whether you pay in full or carry a balance, shapes what it costs you.

reveal.text: The rate includes the bank's own estimate of the chance of not being repaid.

lead.text: Many cards advertise **interest-free days**, a number of days in which you are not charged interest on purchases. They come with a condition: the days apply only when the whole balance is paid by the due date. A card with 55 interest-free days does not give you 55 free days on whatever you choose to pay. It gives them to the holder who clears the whole statement balance on time.

Someone who pays in full every month therefore never pays the purchase rate at all, and can choose a card for its days. Someone who carries a balance never gets the days and pays the rate on what is left, so for them the rate and the annual fee are what matter.

afterFigure.text: That is why Moneysmart tells people to decide first how they will use a card: pay the full balance each month, carry a balance sometimes, or use rewards and travel benefits. The best card is different for each.

steps.headline: Matching a card to its use

lead.text: Take two invented cards. Card A offers up to 55 interest-free days, an annual fee of $120 and a purchase rate of 21%. Card B is a no-frills card with up to 25 interest-free days, an annual fee of $59 and a purchase rate of 13%. Moneysmart's advice for someone who always pays in full is to consider a card with more interest-free days, even if its rate and annual fee are higher, because the full payer never pays the rate. For someone who expects to carry a balance, it suggests a no-frills card with a lower rate and a low annual fee, since lower interest saves money over time.

The two views in the figure mark what each holder should look at. The full payer looks at the days, and weighs the extra $61 of annual fee against 30 more days. The holder who carries a balance looks at the rate and the fee, because the rate is charged on the balance every year.

reveal.text: The pattern of use tells you which number on the card is the one that will be paid.

steps.headline: Which invented card costs Ravi less over a year if he keeps $2,500 on it?

lead.text: The method is to work out the interest on the balance for each card, add the annual fee and compare the totals. The interest is roughly the rate times the balance, since the exact charge depends on how the card works out interest.

workedSteps.text: Card A charges 21% on the balance.
Add Card A's annual fee of $120.
Card B charges 13% and has a $59 fee.
Compare the totals.
workedSteps.math: $645 − $384 = $261, about $260 a year in Card B's favour

steps.headline: What do the two invented cards cost Mia over a year if she pays her full balance every month?

lead.text: Mia is the other kind of holder, so the working is different. Two of the lines are left for you.

workedSteps.text: Mia pays the full balance by the due date every month. Say what that does to the purchase rates.
That leaves the annual fee as the only money cost on each card.
The difference in fees is the price of Card A's extra interest-free days.
Say what Mia should weigh when she chooses between the cards.

lead.text: Rewards cards give points for spending, and the points have a price. Moneysmart's example is Jen, who would get one reward point for each dollar she spends. Joining the program costs $30 a year, and a $25 gift card would take $5,700 of spending. She decides against it, because the cost would be greater than what the rewards are worth.

The figures show how to make the judgement. A $25 reward for $5,700 of spending returns under half a cent for each dollar, about 0.44c, so even before any extra interest the reward is worth less than the $30 fee. At that rate Jen would have to spend about $6,840 a year just to earn back the fee. Moneysmart adds that rewards cards can cost more, especially for someone who does not pay the full balance each month, so the value of the rewards belongs next to the higher fees and rates.

reveal.text: A reward is worth having only if it is worth more than the fee and the extra rate that come with it.

steps.headline: Paying down more than one card

lead.text: If you carry a balance, the minimum repayment is not the amount to aim for. Moneysmart says that paying more than the minimum clears the debt sooner and reduces the interest you pay. With more than one card, keep making each card's required repayment and put any extra money towards one card. Putting it on the card with the highest interest rate saves the most interest, and putting it on the smallest balance gives quicker progress, which helps some people keep going.

A **balance transfer**, which moves a debt to a card or loan with a low or 0% introductory rate, can also help, but only under conditions. Moneysmart warns that it may not save money if the debt is not paid off during the introductory period, and says to check the fees, the rate and the repayment period before applying.

reveal.text: Each extra dollar saves the rate of the card it goes to, so the dearest debt comes first.

lessons.orientation: Say what a credit card costs for a given pattern of use, choose between two cards for someone who pays in full and someone who carries a balance, and judge whether a rewards program is worth its fee.
lessons.nextAction: Read the conditions of interest-free deals and buy now pay later services to find what they really cost.

blocks.text: Australians hold about 14.7 million credit cards between them, with about $33 billion owing on those cards. According to the figures that the Reserve Bank publishes and Moneysmart repeats, somewhere between $18 billion and $19 billion of that is accruing interest, at an average rate of over 18% a year.

Those numbers describe two kinds of holder: people who pay each bill in full and never pay interest, and people who carry a balance and pay it all the time. Which kind you are decides what a good card looks like, and a card that suits one can cost the other a great deal.

intro.promise: By the end you'll say what a card costs for a given way of using it, choose a card for a full payer and for a balance carrier, and judge a rewards program.
intro.whyItMatters: A card that suits one holder can cost another hundreds of dollars a year, and the two cases look alike until you ask how the card will be used.

recap.keyIdea: What a card costs depends on how it is used: interest-free days help only a holder who pays in full, the rate and fee decide the cost for one who carries a balance, and rewards pay only when they beat their fees.

blocks.text: You priced two invented cards for a holder who carries $2,500 and for one who pays in full, and saw that [[interest-free days|Days with no interest on purchases, which apply only if the full balance is paid by the due date. Met in 'Credit cards'.]] are worth something only to the second. Jen's $30 fee against a $25 reward showed how to test a rewards program, and Hana's three cards showed that extra repayments go first to the card with the highest rate.

recap.nextHook: Next we look at interest-free offers and buy now pay later, where the cost sits in the conditions.

lessons.title: Interest-free offers and buy now pay later

lead.text: An **interest-free deal** lets you take goods home and pay for them in stages, over 12, 24 or 60 months for example, with no interest charged during that time. The deal is normally tied to a store card or a credit card, and the retailer who sells it to you is not the lender on the contract, so the contract is where the real terms are. An interest-free deal can still cost money: you may pay an establishment fee, a payment processing fee, an account-keeping fee, an annual fee on the card or a late fee. Some deals also require a store card or credit card, and then you should find out what interest rate applies once the promotional period is over.

The headline is therefore only the first line of an offer. The figure sets two invented offers for the same $3,000 couch side by side. Both say 24 months interest free, and the cost sits in the lines underneath: which card you need, what fees you pay, how much you repay each month and what happens at the end.

afterFigure.text: Moneysmart's advice is to work out the total you will pay, including any fees, before you sign.

lead.text: Interest-free deals come with three styles of repayment. With equal instalments you pay the same amount every month, and the payments add up to the amount borrowed. With a **minimum repayment** they fall short: paying only the minimum leaves part of the total unpaid when the interest-free period ends, so you have to clear the balance before then to avoid interest. With a deferred payment you pay nothing until the end of the period.

How big is the gap? On the couch, equal instalments of $125 a month, which is $3,000 divided by 24, bring the balance to nothing at month 24, while the $60 minimum brings it down only to $1,560. If you still owe money at that point, the remaining balance may start to attract interest, at rates Moneysmart says can be as high as 29%, which is higher than the average credit card. At 29%, $1,560 would cost roughly $450 over a year, and the lender does not have to remind you when the period ends.

afterFigure.text: Moneysmart's tip follows from the figure: split the balance by the number of months in the period and pay that amount each month, and nothing is left owing at the end.

steps.headline: Does a $50 minimum clear a $2,400 interest-free deal over 12 months, and what payment would?

lead.text: The figures are invented. The method is to add up what the minimum repays over the whole period, compare that with the price, and then work out the payment that would clear it.

workedSteps.text: Add up what the minimum repayments come to over the whole period.
Compare that with the price. If it is smaller, the minimum will not clear the deal.
workedSteps.math: $600 is less than $2,400, so $1,800 is left

workedSteps.text: Divide the price by the number of months to find the payment that would clear it.
Compare it with the minimum to see how far the minimum falls short.

lead.text: **Buy now pay later**, or BNPL, lets you take a product now and spread the payments over time. A small purchase is usually paid off within a few weeks, and a big one can take several years. You usually pay no interest on the purchase and are charged fees instead: a late fee, a fixed monthly account-keeping fee, an extra processing fee that some services add to each payment, and an establishment fee for opening the account. Many are advertised as having no interest at all, and some arrangements must cap the fees they charge, which the contract will show.

Two more costs come from outside the service. Your bank may charge an overdrawn fee if your account lacks the money for a scheduled repayment, and if you pay by credit card you pay the card's interest. Every application also triggers a credit check, and late or missed payments can be reported and lower your credit score, which lenders look at when you apply for a home loan or a car loan.

reveal.text: The service charges for running the arrangement, and the bank and the card charge for what happens to the money.

lead.text: Georgia's story, from Moneysmart, shows what happens when the safeguards are skipped. In the lead-up to Christmas she buys a $150 pair of sneakers and splits the payments with one BNPL service. She then finds a $300 hair straightener at another store and uses a different service for it. A fortnight later her bank account is overdrawn, because she had not checked whether she could cover both repayments.

Moneysmart's tips for BNPL are to keep to a spending limit you can afford, stick to a single service at a time, include the instalments in your budget alongside bills and loan repayments, and link the service to a debit card, so that the money is your own and no card interest is added. It also notes that several services at once are hard to keep track of, and that lay-by carries neither account-keeping nor late fees.

reveal.text: The overdrawn fee came from the account, not from the services, so the safeguard is a check before buying.

lead.text: Moneysmart reports a Federal Court ruling from July 2026 that set penalties of $35 million for Harvey Norman Holdings Ltd and $20 million for Latitude Finance Australia, over misleading conduct in a national advertising campaign. The campaign promoted paying for goods at Harvey Norman stores through a 60-month deal with no interest and no deposit. The Court found it misleading because buyers were not adequately told that they needed a specified credit card and had to pay fees.

The headline said 60 months with no interest and no deposit, and the conditions that changed the cost, the required card and the fees, were not adequately disclosed. Reading an offer means finding those conditions yourself, so work out the total you will pay including fees, and check which interest rate applies once the promotional period ends.

reveal.text: Where an offer is honest about its conditions, you can price it. Where it is not, the headline tells you nothing.

lead.text: Moneysmart says there is no need to feel pressured by a 'limited time' interest-free offer, and it lists other ways to pay. A No Interest Loan can help a person on a low income pay for essential household items, and it carries no interest or fees, so you repay only what you borrowed. Lay-by lets you pay for an item in equal repayments with no interest, although you cannot take the item home right away. Saving up avoids borrowing altogether.

Each option has its own conditions, so the same two questions apply to all of them: what do the conditions add to the price, and what happens if you cannot pay on time? Moneysmart adds that if you are struggling to meet repayments on an interest-free deal you can contact the lender, and that you can apply to have the loan made more manageable because of financial hardship.

reveal.text: The cheapest route is the one with the fewest conditions, and it is slower.

lessons.orientation: Work out what an interest-free or buy now pay later offer will cost under its conditions, and find the condition that turns 'free' into a debt.
lessons.reviewLabel: Interest-free offers and buy now pay later

blocks.text: A shop advertises a $3,000 couch with 24 months interest free. The fine print gives a minimum repayment of $60 a month, and a buyer who pays exactly the minimum and never misses a month assumes that is all there is to it. The figures are invented, but the structure is the one Moneysmart describes for offers of this kind.

The headline promises no interest, and the conditions decide what that promise is worth. Reading them takes some arithmetic and a short list of questions, and the same questions apply to the instalment services that many shops offer at the checkout.

intro.promise: By the end you'll work out what an interest-free or buy now pay later offer costs under its conditions, and find the condition that turns free into a debt.
intro.whyItMatters: The headline of an offer says what is free, and the conditions say what is not, so the cost sits in a few lines that are easy to skip.

recap.keyIdea: An interest-free or buy now pay later offer costs what its conditions say, so check the card, the fees and what happens at the end, and compare the minimum repayments with the price, because a balance left at the end can attract interest.

blocks.text: You saw that $60 a month on a $3,000 deal leaves $1,560 after 24 months, and that splitting the price by the months gives the payment that clears it. [[Buy now pay later|Paying by instalments, usually with fees instead of interest. Met in 'Interest-free offers and buy now pay later'.]] has costs of its own, from late fees to the overdrawn fees a bank adds when two services draw on one account. The Federal Court's finding on a 60-month advertisement shows why the required card and the fees belong in the price you work out.

recap.nextHook: Next we look at HECS-HELP, a debt with its own repayment table and an indexation rate that works like interest.

lessons.title: HECS-HELP

lead.text: HELP is the Higher Education Loan Program, one of several study and training loans whose compulsory repayments the ATO sets out in a single table. The table is read against your **repayment income**, which is your taxable income with some amounts added: reportable fringe benefits, any net investment loss (net rental losses included), reportable super contributions and exempt foreign employment income.

The figure shows the table for the 2026-27 income year. Nothing is repaid up to $69,528. Above that, each dollar of repayment income adds 15c to the repayment until $129,717, where the repayment has reached $9,028. Above $129,717 each dollar adds 17c, and from $186,051 the repayment is 10% of the whole repayment income.

afterFigure.text: The thresholds are updated every year, so a figure is worth quoting only with its year. The 2025-26 table, for instance, started charging above $67,000.

diagram.alt: A scale of repayment income from $0 to $220,000 split at $69,528, $129,717 and $186,050 into four bands: nothing to repay, 15c on each dollar over $69,528, a base of $9,028 plus 17c on each dollar over $129,717, and 10% of the whole income. The second case marks an income of $86,380 in the 15c band.

steps.headline: What is Christina's compulsory repayment for 2026-27?

lead.text: This is the ATO's own example for the 2026-27 income year. Christina has $16,500 in reportable super contributions, $60,470 of taxable income, $5,400 of reportable fringe benefits, $2,680 of exempt foreign employment income and a net investment loss of $1,330.

workedSteps.text: Add every amount on the ATO's list to find her repayment income.
That falls in the 15c row, which charges only the part over $69,528, so take the threshold away first.
Take 15c on each of those dollars.
Her repayment is $2,527.80, just under 3% of her repayment income and a long way below the 15c headline rate.

lead.text: From the 2025-26 income year the ATO works out compulsory repayments with marginal rates, so each rate is charged only on the income above that row's threshold. A raise is therefore priced at the [[marginal rate|The rate on the next dollar earned. Met in 'From gross pay to take-home'.]] of the row it lands in, which in the middle band is 15c for each extra dollar.

Take a repayment income of $85,000 in 2026-27. The repayment is 15% of the $15,472 over $69,528, which is $2,320.80. At $90,000 it is 15% of $20,472, which is $3,070.80. The extra $5,000 of income added $750, which is **15c on each of its dollars** and nothing more.

afterFigure.text: The line bends at each threshold but never jumps. Even where the table switches to 10% of the whole income at $186,051, the repayment is within a dollar of what the row above gives, about $18,600 at $186,050, so a raise is never penalised by crossing a line.

lead.text: Repayments are one side of a HELP debt. The other side is that an unpaid balance grows, and the ATO's word for the yearly increase is **indexation**. On 1 June each year it is applied to the part of the loan that has been unpaid for over 11 months, so a sum borrowed in March is not indexed on the next 1 June while the older part of the debt is. The rate follows the change in the [[CPI|The Consumer Price Index, which tracks how prices change. Met in 'Compounding, inflation and time'.]] or in the Wage Price Index, whichever is lower, and the ATO says this keeps the real value of the loan.

Indexation is not called interest, but Study Assist, the Department of Education's guide to study loans, says that, like interest, it means your debt grows over time. In 2026 the rate is 2.8%, so $20,000 that had been unpaid for more than 11 months on 1 June 2026 gains $560. That is what happens to Mia's $20,000 while she repays nothing.

The ATO's table of indexation rates shows two years with a second number beside them: 2024 reads 4% (previously 4.7%) and 2023 reads 3.2% (previously 7.1%). The second numbers are the rates those years carried before a change in how indexation is calculated. Legislation passed in November 2024 moved it to the lower of the CPI and the Wage Price Index, and the change was backdated to 1 June 2023, so both years were restated.
On a $20,000 debt the gap between 7.1% and 3.2% is the gap between $1,420 and $640, which is $780 for a single year.

afterFigure.text: The settled rates run from 2.8% in 2026 to 4% in 2024. The 7.1% that 2023 carried before the change was the highest rate in the figure.

lead.text: A voluntary repayment made before 1 June reduces the part of the debt that indexation is applied to. Study Assist advises paying voluntarily no later than 5 business days before 1 June, and says the debt then accrues a smaller amount of indexation.

What it saves is the indexation rate on the amount repaid. A $5,000 voluntary repayment avoids 2.8% of $5,000, which is $140 at the 2026 rate. Set that beside a credit card charging 19%, a made-up rate close to the average of over 18% that ASIC's Moneysmart site reports for cards as at May 2026: $5,000 left on the card for a year costs about $950 in interest, nearly seven times as much.

afterFigure.text: Each repayment saves the rate on the amount repaid, whoever the lender is, so the same dollars do more against a 19% debt than against a 2.8% one.

blocks.text: Mia borrowed through HELP for her degree several years ago and still owes $20,000. This year her pay is low enough that she makes no repayment at all. An unpaid bank loan would keep growing with its interest, so what do you expect her HELP debt to do?

The answer tells you what it costs to carry the debt, and that cost is what you compare with every other debt in this course. The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) publishes the figures, along with the table that decides what repaying takes from pay.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what repaying HELP takes from a given income, and what each year of not repaying adds.
intro.whyItMatters: The ATO publishes both figures, so you can check any claim about HELP against them.

recap.keyIdea: A HELP repayment is charged only on repayment income above each threshold, and an unpaid debt grows by indexation, which was 2.8% in 2026.

blocks.text: You read the ATO's 2026-27 table against a repayment income that adds more than taxable income, and priced a raise at the rate of the row it lands in, which is 15c on each extra dollar in the middle band. You also saw that [[indexation|The yearly 1 June increase to the part of a HELP debt unpaid for more than 11 months. Met in 'Indexation'.]] is applied to the part of the debt unpaid for more than 11 months, that two years of the rate were restated, and that a repaid $5,000 saves about $950 on a 19% card against about $140 of indexation.

recap.nextHook: Next is the home loan, and what a rate or an offset account is worth in dollars a year.

lessons.title: Home loans and offset accounts

lead.text: Why would two lenders charge different rates for the same loan? The RBA explains that a bank sets its lending rates to make its lending as profitable as it can, within what it judges to be an appropriate exposure to borrowers who fail to repay. Three things feed into that: what the bank pays to fund its loans, how likely it thinks a borrower is to repay, and how hard it has to compete for borrowers.

On competition, the RBA says that when borrowers want to borrow less than banks want to lend, banks have to compete to attract them, and all else equal more competition typically means lower lending rates. ASIC's Moneysmart site reported in September 2026 that variable rates on offer can differ by more than 2 percentage points across the market, which on $600,000 would be more than $12,000 a year. A **variable rate** can go up or down, while a **fixed rate** holds at one figure for a set period, commonly one to five years.

afterFigure.text: A rate gap is worth looking for because it applies to every year of the loan. Moneysmart's own example is a rate 0.2% lower, which it says could save thousands of dollars over time, and on $600,000 each 0.2% is the $1,200 a year you sized at the start.

lead.text: The usual home loan is a **principal and interest** loan: each repayment pays the interest owing and also pays down some of the amount borrowed, which is the principal. The **term** is the number of years over which the loan is repaid, and it sets how the two trade off. A shorter term, such as 25 years, means higher repayments and less interest overall, and a longer one, such as 30 years, means lower repayments and more interest.

Take two made-up loans of $600,000 at about 6%. The standard repayment formula gives about $3,600 a month over 30 years and about $3,870 over 25 years. The 25-year loan costs about $270 more each month, but the interest it charges over its life comes to about $560,000 against about $695,000 for the 30-year loan, some $135,000 less, because the balance falls faster and the interest stops five years sooner.

afterFigure.text: An interest-only loan goes furthest in the direction of the lower repayment: during its interest-only period the debt stays exactly where it was.

reveal.text: Notice that the lower payment on the longer loan was paid for with ten more years of interest, not with a lower rate.

lead.text: An **offset account** is an everyday account tied to a home loan, usually a variable-rate one, and its balance is taken off the loan balance before interest is worked out. Moneysmart's example is a $750,000 loan with $50,000 in the offset account, which is charged interest on $700,000. Interest on most loans is worked out daily on the loan balance less the offset balance, so the saving is the loan rate applied to whatever sits in the account.

That puts the saving into a single multiplication. On a $600,000 loan at 6%, an average of $30,000 in the offset saves 6% of $30,000, which is $1,800 a year. The offset does not pay you interest: it lowers the interest the lender charges you, and the money stays in an account you can still use. A **redraw** facility works differently, because extra repayments go onto the loan itself and whether you can withdraw them again depends on the loan's terms.

afterFigure.text: Both lower the balance that interest is charged on. What an offset adds is access to the savings, and what it may cost is a higher rate or a fee for the feature.

lead.text: Every lender must give you a Key Facts Sheet for a loan, and the layout is the same whichever lender it comes from, which is what lets you set two offers side by side. It shows the interest rate, a comparison rate personalised to you, the total you would pay back, the monthly repayment, the establishment fee and any ongoing fees.

The figure shows two made-up sheets from one lender, with the fees set at nothing so that only the rate and an offset account differ. Loan Y has the lower rate and the lower repayment, and Loan X has the offset.

afterFigure.text: The sheet cannot say which loan is cheaper for you, because that depends on how much you would keep in the offset. The next screens put that into dollars.

steps.headline: Raj keeps about $20,000 in savings. Which is cheaper for him on $600,000, Loan X at 6.25% with an offset or Loan Y at 6.10% without?

lead.text: Both loans are the made-up ones from the Key Facts figure. The method is to price X's extra rate, price the offset, and compare the two.

workedSteps.text: Loan X's rate is 0.15 points higher, which costs this much each year on the whole loan.
The offset saves the loan rate on the balance Raj keeps in it.
Set the saving against the extra rate.
X is cheaper for Raj by about $350 a year. Its offset covers the extra rate once the balance is large enough to save $900, which is where the break-even lies.

lead.text: Raj kept $20,000 in the offset. Kim keeps less.

reveal.text: The balance in the offset decides it: above about $14,400 Loan X wins, below it Loan Y does.

lead.text: How would you know whether an offset is working? Not from the repayment. Moneysmart reports a review by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) in which some banks had failed to link their customers' offset accounts to their loans.

It gives the example of James and Mia, who have a $750,000 loan on a $1 million home over 30 years at 6.25%, with an average of $50,000 in their offset. Their bank failed to link it, so they paid over $3,000 more interest in a year, which matches 6.25% of $50,000. Had it gone unnoticed for the whole 30 years, they would have given up nearly $230,000 of interest savings and taken four extra years to pay the loan off. Their repayments stayed the same throughout, so nothing in the repayment hinted at it.

afterFigure.text: Moneysmart's advice is to check in the app or on statements that the offset is reducing the interest charged, to ask the bank if your savings are not shown, and to check the link again after refinancing or switching products.

reveal.text: The repayment hides a failed link. The interest charged does not.

lead.text: A variable rate can rise, and Moneysmart suggests working out what your costs would be if rates went up by 3%, which is a **stress test**. On $600,000, 3 percentage points is $18,000 more interest in the first year, about $1,500 a month, and a little less in practice as the balance falls.

Extra repayments work in the other direction. In the early years most of each repayment is interest, so extra payments made then reduce the interest over the life of the loan the most. Paying half the monthly amount every two weeks gives 26 half-payments a year, which equals an extra month of repayments, and if you switch to a cheaper rate while paying the same amount as before, the loan is paid off sooner.

afterFigure.text: Before you sign, Moneysmart also suggests asking about extra repayments, about break costs, and about what happens when a fixed or introductory rate ends.

lead.text: A new case: a low rate that does not last.

reveal.text: Moneysmart's question is what happens when the introductory rate ends, and the answer has to be weighed over the years you keep the loan.

blocks.text: Two lenders will lend you the same $600,000, one at 6.00% a year and the other at 6.20%. A gap of 0.2% sounds too small to bother with, and most choices in a home loan look that small, whether it is a fraction of a point on the rate or a feature that costs a little extra.
Each of them can be put into dollars a year with a single multiplication, which is how you tell the ones that matter from the ones that don't. Start with the gap between those two lenders.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to put a rate or an offset account into dollars a year, and check that an offset is working.
intro.whyItMatters: A fraction of a point on $600,000 is worth hundreds or thousands of dollars every year.

recap.keyIdea: A rate gap applies to the whole loan, an offset saves the loan rate only on the balance held in it, and a longer term lowers the repayment while adding interest.

blocks.text: You sized a 0.2% gap at $1,200 a year on $600,000, and found that an [[offset account|A transaction account linked to a home loan, whose balance is taken off the loan balance before interest is worked out. Met in 'Offset accounts'.]] holding $30,000 saves $1,800 a year at 6%. Whether an offset beats a lower rate depends on the balance you keep, and Kim's $8,000 was too small for it. The interest charged, and not the repayment, shows whether the link is working, and a 3 point rise in rates is worth about $18,000 a year in extra interest on $600,000.

recap.nextHook: Next is superannuation: who pays into it, how each kind of contribution is taxed and capped, and when the money can come out.

lessons.title: How super works

lead.text: Who decides how much goes into super? For most employees the answer is a law. The Hawke government brought in the super guarantee to encourage people to fund more of their own retirement and lean less on a publicly funded pension, and the law that put it into effect passed in 1992. Employers must put a percentage of your pay into a super fund for you. That percentage was 9.00% from 2002 to 2013, and it then climbed in steps.

The figure shows the general rate for each period in the ATO's table. It reached 12.00% in 2025-26, which is also the rate for 2026-27, and the table has it staying at 12.00% from 1 July 2027 onwards.

afterFigure.text: The guarantee is paid **on top of** an employee's pay and is not part of the wage or salary, so Aisha's pay stays $80,000 and about $9,600 is added to her super. From 1 July 2026 employers must pay it for each payday.

lead.text: A percentage needs something to be a percentage of. Until 30 June 2026 the guarantee was worked out on ordinary time earnings, and from 1 July 2026 it is worked out on **qualifying earnings**, which are the payments the ATO says are used to calculate it under Payday Super. They include ordinary time earnings, which is pay for ordinary hours together with some paid leave, allowances, bonuses and lump sums, and also all commissions and any salary sacrifice amounts that would have counted.

The ATO says that overtime is generally not part of ordinary time earnings or qualifying earnings, so a worker whose pay includes overtime gets a guarantee of less than 12% of everything they are paid. Ben earns $70,000 in ordinary pay and $6,000 in overtime in a year: his guarantee is 12% of $70,000, which is $8,400, and not 12% of $76,000, which would be $9,120.

Money reaches super in two ways, and the tax treatment depends on which. A **concessional contribution** is money that has not been taxed as your income: employer contributions, including the guarantee and any salary sacrifice, and personal contributions that you claim as a tax deduction. The fund pays 15% tax on most of these, called contributions tax. For most people that is less than the income tax on the same money, which is the concession that the word concessional refers to. As of September 2026, ASIC's Moneysmart site adds that someone earning up to $37,000 may have it refunded by the government, and that someone whose income plus concessional contributions is over $250,000 pays a further 15%, called Division 293 tax.

A **non-concessional contribution** is a personal contribution from after-tax money for which you do not claim a deduction. It comes from money that has already been taxed as income, and it has a cap of its own, $130,000 for 2026-27. Claiming a deduction on a personal contribution turns it into a concessional one.
Each payment belongs to one of the two kinds.

reveal.text: The two kinds of contribution are counted against separate caps, so a large non-concessional payment does not use up the concessional cap.

lead.text: How much can go in at the concessional rate? For 2026-27 the usual **concessional contributions cap** is $32,500 a year, up from $30,000, because it is indexed to average weekly ordinary time earnings. It counts employer contributions, including salary sacrifice, and personal contributions you claim as a deduction. If you hold more than one fund, everything paid to all of them counts together, and so do costs your employer pays to a fund for you, for example administration fees and insurance premiums.

The employer's 12% therefore uses part of the cap before you add anything. Tom earns $90,000, so his employer pays $10,800 and he has $21,700 of room. Sacrificing a further $15,000 keeps him under the cap with $6,700 to spare, while sacrificing $25,000 takes him $3,300 over.

afterFigure.text: The ATO says that contributing more than the caps may mean paying extra tax, and Wikipedia adds that the excess is taxed at the person's ordinary marginal rate, so there is no tax benefit in going over. Unused cap from recent years can sometimes be carried forward, but the questions in this lesson assume there is none.

steps.headline: Omar earns $100,000 and Lin $40,000 in 2026-27. Each salary-sacrifices $1,000. About how much tax does each save, against taking it as pay?

lead.text: Salary sacrifice sends part of pay to super before it is taxed as income, so the saving is the income tax avoided less the 15% the fund charges. The rates below include the 2% Medicare levy, and the working ignores tax offsets and Division 293 tax.

workedSteps.text: Find the rate each pays on the next dollar in the 2026-27 table, then add the levy.
Take away the 15% the fund charges on a concessional contribution.
Apply each result to the $1,000 sacrificed.
Omar saves about $170 and Lin about $20, so the saving follows the gap between the marginal rate and 15%.

lead.text: A new case: one earner is in a higher band.

reveal.text: The gap between the marginal rate and 15% widens as income rises through the bands, so the saving does too.

lead.text: Super is preserved, which means you can withdraw it only when a condition of release is met. The ATO lists four: turning 65, even if you are still working; reaching your preservation age and retiring; reaching your preservation age and moving to a transition to retirement income stream while you carry on working; and satisfying one of the conditions for early access.

Your preservation age is set by your date of birth, and the figure shows it rising from 55 to 60. Moneysmart reports that from age 60 an income stream is usually tax-free, and so is a lump sum from a taxed fund.

diagram.caption: The ATO's preservation ages. Anyone born from 1 July 1964 has a preservation age of 60.

lead.text: Because the money is locked away, some people sell a way round that. The ATO warns that promoters may offer to start a self-managed super fund (SMSF) so that you can take your super out to pay for credit card debt, a house or car, or a holiday. Withdrawing super without meeting a condition of release is illegal, and the ATO says the cost of taking part is far more than the super released.

Any amount you access illegally counts as income on your tax return, and it still counts if you put the money back into the fund, so you may also pay tax shortfall penalties and interest. If someone tells you to set up an SMSF, the ATO says to check that they are a licensed financial adviser on ASIC's Moneysmart website.
Read the extract before you answer.

reveal.text: The promoter's promise to 'put it back' is the part of the offer that sounds safest, and it is the part the extract speaks to.

lessons.orientation: Say who pays into super, how each kind of contribution is taxed and capped, and when the money can be taken out, then judge a contribution or an early-access offer.
