blocks.text: Aisha has been offered $80,000 a year for her first full-time job, and the contract says her employer will also pay super at 12%. She wonders whether the 12% will come out of the $80,000 or be added to it.

Super goes into a fund she cannot normally touch until she is much older, so how the money gets there, how it is taxed and how much can go in each year all decide what she ends up with. The ATO publishes the figures for each of those.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to sort contributions, test one against the 2026-27 cap, and spot an offer to release super early.
intro.whyItMatters: The same $1,000 is worth different amounts to different people, depending on the kind of contribution and their income.

recap.keyIdea: Super is paid on top of pay at 12%, taxed at 15% in the fund, capped each year, and preserved until a condition of release is met.

blocks.text: You saw that the guarantee rose from 9.00% to 12.00% and is paid on top of pay, that [[concessional contributions|Contributions that count towards the $32,500 cap: employer payments, salary sacrifice and personal payments claimed as a deduction. Met in 'Two kinds of contribution'.]] include the employer's payment, and that the employer's share leaves less room under the cap than it first seems. A salary sacrifice saves the gap between your marginal rate and the 15% charged in the fund, which was about $170 for Omar and $20 for Lin on $1,000. Early-access schemes are illegal, and money put back in the fund is still taxed as income.

recap.nextHook: Next is what a super fund charges, and how to compare two funds fairly.

lessons.title: Super fees and choosing a fund

lead.text: Every super fund charges fees, and a fee can be a set dollar amount, a percentage of your balance or a mix of the two, taken regularly, often weekly or monthly. ASIC's Moneysmart site lists the names you will meet: administration fees, which include advice from the fund about your own account, investment fees, buy/sell spreads, transaction costs, switching fees and personal advice fees. Funds also charge when you switch.

Moneysmart's summary is that when two funds perform equally well, the one with lower fees usually leaves you with a faster-growing balance. The next screen shows how a difference that looks small adds up.

Moneysmart's example is Savannah, who is 30, earns $50,000 a year and has $20,000 in super, paying 2.5% in fees. She switches to a fund that charges 1% for the same level of performance. Moneysmart's figures put her balance at 65 at $336,000 instead of $255,000, which is $81,000 more.

Why does a gap of 1.5 points turn into so much? A fee of 2.5% takes 2.5 cents of every dollar in the account each year, whatever the fund earned. As the account grows the dollars taken grow with it, and each dollar taken in an early year stops earning for all the years after. **The gap is charged every year, on a growing balance**, so across 35 years it builds into a large share of the final balance.

afterFigure.text: Moneysmart's figures are one example, with their own assumptions about returns and contributions, so another member's gap would differ. What carries over to any member is that the fee is charged every year.

steps.headline: How much bigger is Savannah's balance in the 1% fund, as a share of the balance in the 2.5% fund?

lead.text: The question is about the gap in proportion to the balance it is compared with, so the working finds the gap first and then divides.

workedSteps.text: Find the gap between the two balances at 65.
Compare the gap with the smaller balance, because the question asks how much bigger the larger one is.
That is about 32%, or roughly a third, far more than the 1.5 points of the fee gap.

lead.text: Think about how long each member pays the gap.

reveal.text: A fee gap is charged every year, so the number of years left is a main driver of what it costs.

lead.text: When you start a job your employer must offer you a choice of fund. If you choose none, the employer checks with the ATO to see whether you already have one, which is called your **stapled fund**, and pays into that. If you have no fund yet, as in a first job, the employer pays into a default product that it chose.

Since 1 January 2014 default contributions have had to go only into an authorised MySuper product, which Wikipedia describes as a simple, low-cost design with a short list of standard fees and one balanced investment option. Most employees' super sits in large funds of two kinds: industry funds, which are not-for-profit and run by boards of industry stakeholders, and retail funds, which are for-profit and run by financial institutions.

To compare funds fairly, Moneysmart suggests looking at performance over the past five years or longer, and comparing similar options over the same timeframe, such as one fund's balanced option with another's. Past performance is not a guarantee. A fund must tell you if it fails APRA's yearly performance test (APRA is the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority), and the ATO's YourSuper comparison tool compares MySuper products.

Moneysmart also points out that comparison websites are businesses, that they may be paid for promoted links and that they score funds differently, so one website's rating should not be the only basis for a choice. The figure shows three invented funds.

afterFigure.text: A higher potential return usually comes with a higher risk of loss, so the highest return in a table often belongs to the riskiest option, and the kind of option has to match before the numbers are compared.

reveal.text: Matching the kind of option and the period comes before comparing the returns or the fees.

lead.text: If you have changed jobs you may hold more than one super account, and each can charge fees and insurance premiums, so you may be paying duplicates. Insurance premiums come out of the balance. Combining your accounts into one can make them easier to manage and may save on fees and insurance, and Moneysmart says you can see how many accounts you hold, and merge them at no cost, through the ATO in myGov.

The caution is that closing an account can end the insurance it carried. Moneysmart's example is Kristin, who had worked several casual jobs and found three accounts in three funds. She used the YourSuper tool to compare fees and ten-year performance, and then moved her super into the account she preferred through myGov.

reveal.text: Moneysmart's advice is to check for insurance you want to keep before you combine accounts.

lessons.orientation: Size what a fee difference is worth by retirement, and compare two funds fairly on like-for-like options, fees, insurance and performance over the same period.

blocks.text: Savannah is 30, earns $50,000 a year and has $20,000 in super, in a fund that charges 2.5% a year in fees. She finds another fund with the same investment performance that charges 1%. The gap is 1.5 percentage points, which looks too small to bother about.
Fees come out every year, on a balance that is growing, so the gap is charged on more money each year. Before seeing how fees are charged, make a guess at what it adds up to by the time she is 65.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to size a fee gap against a final balance and compare two funds fairly.
intro.whyItMatters: A fee gap of 1.5 points a year changed Savannah's balance at 65 by $81,000.

recap.keyIdea: A fee is charged every year on a growing balance, so a small gap becomes a large share of the final balance, and funds are compared fairly only like for like over five years or more.

blocks.text: In Moneysmart's example a 1.5 point fee gap left Savannah with $81,000 more at 65, about a third of the smaller balance, because the gap is charged each year for 35 years. To compare funds, set the same kind of option over the same period side by side, and treat one website's rating as one opinion. Before you [[combine accounts|Moving several super accounts into one. Met in 'Several accounts'.]], check for insurance you want to keep, and if you choose no fund your employer uses your stapled fund or else a default product.

recap.nextHook: Next is risk and return, and how the time before you need the money decides what suits it.

lessons.title: Risk, return and time

lead.text: What is Maya buying when she buys into a fund? ASIC's Moneysmart site sorts investments into four classes. Shares are part ownership of a company, and they have historically returned more than the other traditional classes, but they are more likely than the others to fall in value in a given year. Bonds, also called fixed income, are loans to governments or companies, with lower returns and a smaller chance of falling. Property earns rental income and can grow in value, and for most people it means the family home. Cash has a low risk of loss, and inflation reduces what it buys.
The figure sets the four side by side with the way each can lose money and the time frame Moneysmart gives as a guide.

afterFigure.text: No class is free of risk. Moneysmart says that no investment is completely risk-free, and that spreading money across classes means relying less on any one of them but does not remove the risk of loss.

diagram.alt: A table of four asset classes. Shares are more likely to fall in value in a given year and suit the long term, at least 5 years. Property can fall in value and generally suits at least 5 years. Bonds can fall when interest rates rise or the borrower may fail to pay, and no time frame is given. Cash has a low risk of loss but inflation reduces what it buys, and suits goals within 3 years.
diagram.caption: From Moneysmart's pages on asset classes and time frames. Shares and property are growth assets, and cash and some bonds are defensive.

lead.text: Moneysmart groups the classes by what they are for. **Defensive** investments, such as cash and some bonds, aim to protect your money, to provide income or both. Their potential returns are lower, and they can still lose money, so they suit people who need the money soon or who could not afford a large fall. **Growth** investments, such as shares and property, aim to grow in value over many years, and they suit longer goals if you can cope with larger falls.
Investments that could earn more usually also carry a bigger chance of losing money, so a high return on offer is a sign of a high risk of loss.
Bonds are a defensive-leaning class. Ask what can move their price.

reveal.text: A defensive investment aims to protect money, and it can still lose some. Cash is the one with a low risk of loss.

lead.text: Time decides how much of a fall you can sit through. Moneysmart's guide is that cash is the usual home for money needed soon, within about 3 years, and that shares and property generally suit goals at least 5 years away. Money needed in 18 months cannot wait for a recovery that might take longer, while money needed in 12 years has more time to wait out a fall.

Moneysmart adds that these time frames are only a rough guide, and that nothing in them promises an investment will earn money or climb back after a drop, so a long time frame makes growth assets suitable and leaves them as risky as before.

reveal.text: The time frames help you match a goal to an investment, and they do not promise that a fall will be recovered.

lead.text: Most funds hold a mix of growth and defensive assets. Moneysmart describes a growth mix as about 85% growth assets, a balanced mix as about 70% and a conservative mix as about 30%, with a cash option at 100% cash. A super fund's growth option invests more in shares and has a higher risk of losses in some years, a balanced option invests across assets for moderate returns and risk, and a conservative option focuses on protecting the balance, with lower risk and returns. So a balanced mix holds mostly growth assets, well over half.

The share of growth assets tells you roughly how bad a bad year can be. If a balanced option's growth assets fall 20% in a year and its defensive assets stay flat, the whole option falls about 70% of 20%, which is 14%.

afterFigure.text: The defensive assets staying flat is an assumption made to size the effect. Defensive assets can lose money as well, so the true fall in a bad year can be larger.

diagram.alt: Three bars for the conservative, balanced and growth mixes, each split into growth and defensive assets: about 30%, 70% and 85% growth. The second view shows a year in which growth assets fall 20% and defensive assets stay flat, so the whole mix falls about 6%, 14% and 17%.

lead.text: Apply the fall to the growth part only.

reveal.text: The share of growth assets multiplied by their fall gives the fall in the whole option, when the defensive part stays flat.

lead.text: Two different claims are easy to blur. The first is that options with more earning potential usually carry a bigger risk of loss, which Moneysmart describes as the usual pattern. The second is that a particular riskier option will have earned more in a particular period, and Moneysmart says taking on more risk does not ensure a bigger return.

So a single period in which the riskier option came out ahead is one result. It cannot show that the risk was rewarded, any more than a single period in which it came out behind could show that risk never pays.
A new case: one period, two options.

reveal.text: The claim goes further than one result can. Think about what the figures show and what they cannot.

lessons.orientation: Match a goal's time frame to a mix of cash, bonds, shares and property, and say roughly how large a fall a given mix could suffer.
lessons.nextAction: Say whether a portfolio is concentrated, and what diversification and an index fund do and do not remove.

blocks.text: Maya needs $15,000 for a house deposit in 14 months. Her savings account pays little, and in this made-up case a shares fund she has been reading about rose 20% last year. If the same happened again, the fund would turn $15,000 into $18,000.

Whether that is sensible depends on what the fund could do before the day she needs the money, and on what kind of investment it is. Those two things are what a goal's time frame and an asset class tell you.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to match a goal to a kind of investment and say how large a fall a mix could suffer.
intro.whyItMatters: Your time frame decides how much of a fall you can sit through, and last year's return decides nothing.

recap.keyIdea: Match the time you have to the kind of asset, and size a bad year as the share of growth assets times their fall.

blocks.text: Cash and other [[defensive|Investments that aim to protect your money and have lower potential returns, but can still lose money. Met in 'Growth and defensive'.]] assets fit goals within about 3 years, and shares and property generally suit goals at least 5 years away, though no time frame guarantees recovery from a fall. A balanced mix is about 70% growth assets, so a 20% fall in them costs the whole mix about 14%. More risk usually comes with more potential return and a greater risk of loss, and it guarantees nothing, which is why one period's result never proves that risk pays.

recap.nextHook: Next is diversification, and what spreading money across companies does and does not remove.

lessons.title: Diversification, index funds and ETFs

lead.text: Ben's money sits in twenty places, and each place holds a twentieth of it. If one of his companies halves in a year, he loses half of $500, which is $250, or 2.5% of his savings. Mia's one company halving costs her $5,000, half of everything she has. For Ben to lose what Mia loses to one bad company, most of his twenty would have to fall at the same time.

That difference is **diversification**: spreading money so that no single asset or risk can do too much damage. Wikipedia's example is the one in the question. A portfolio of twenty stocks is less likely than one stock to fall by half, and less likely still when the stocks differ in industry, size and kind of asset, since that dilutes whatever is happening in any one of them. Each of Ben's companies is just as risky as Mia's, and what has changed is how much of his money any one of them can take.

Counting holdings is not enough on its own. Moneysmart describes a man called Kyle who owns shares in five mining companies. After a fall in commodity prices his shares lost $5,000, taking them from $25,000 to $20,000, and Moneysmart's comment is that he is taking on a lot of risk because he is not diversified.

The five companies run separate mines under separate managers, so it might seem that Kyle is well spread. The first view of the figure shows why he is not: the price of the commodities they sell moves all five at once. A risk that reaches every company in one industry is called **sector risk**, and a portfolio whose holdings can all be hurt by the same thing is **concentrated**, however many holdings it has. The second view shows five made-up holdings in different sectors facing the same fall, and only the miner is hurt.

afterFigure.text: The test for concentration is how many different things could pull the holdings down together. In the made-up second case the other four sell different things, so a fall in commodity prices leaves them alone, while in Kyle's case nothing cushions it.

diagram.alt: Two views of five holdings drawn as equal bars. In the first, all five are mining companies and all five bars shrink by a fifth after commodity prices fall. In the second, the five holdings are in five different sectors and only the mining bar shrinks.
diagram.caption: Equal bars are for illustration, since Moneysmart gives only Kyle's total. Use the buttons to compare his five miners with five made-up holdings in different sectors.

reveal.text: A fund can be concentrated in the same way. It can hold many companies and still depend on one sector, which comes up again with ETFs.

lead.text: Once the holdings differ in what could hurt them, how many do you need? Fewer than most people expect. Wikipedia describes a study by Edwin Elton and Martin Gruber from 1977, whose result was that the reduction in risk from holding 30 stocks is close to what you get from 1,000, and that even four stocks give most of the reduction compared with holding one.

The shape of that result is what matters. The first few holdings do nearly all the work and the gain from each further one shrinks, so 30 is a point on a curve that has nearly flattened, and nothing makes it a rule.

Past that point, more holdings still cost something. Wikipedia points out, using the proverb about eggs and baskets, that many baskets may cost more to hold, and that when each asset carries a fee, a portfolio can be spread so thin that the fees outweigh what the spreading gains.

reveal.text: What remains after enough holdings is a different kind of risk, one that does not depend on how many holdings you have.

lead.text: If spreading across more companies cannot remove everything, what is left? Take the S&P/ASX 200, the index of Australia's 200 largest companies. If you own one of those companies, you are exposed to two things: what happens to the whole index, and what happens to that company. Own all 200 and the second exposure shrinks to a slice of the result, because no single company's trouble can do more than that, yet the first is still there however many you buy.

Wikipedia names the two. The exposure that exists however many shares you hold is **market risk**, which it calls non-diversifiable, and the exposure to one company's own fortunes is **diversifiable risk**, because spreading can reduce it. [[Sector risk|A risk that reaches every company in one industry at once. Met earlier in this lesson.]] sits in between: more holdings in the same sector leave it where it was, and holdings in other sectors reduce it.

Moneysmart is plain about what this means for a whole portfolio. Spreading money across types of investment means you rely less on any one of them, but it does not remove the risk of loss, and no investment is completely risk-free. Shares have historically returned more than the other traditional types and have a higher chance of falling in any one year, while bonds have lower returns and a smaller chance of falling. Holding some bonds or cash alongside shares can soften a market-wide fall, though nothing takes the risk away.
Moneysmart lists four common ways to spread money. The table gives an example of each and one thing to watch.

Each way answers a different question: what if shares fall, what if one industry does, what if one country's market does. The first three change what you hold, and the fourth, a fund, is a way to get any of them in a single purchase and to pay a fee for it. Overseas holdings that are not hedged against exchange rates carry a risk the others lack, because their value in Australian dollars moves with the exchange rate, and Moneysmart says that can work for or against you.

lead.text: A fund lets someone else do the spreading, and the simplest kind of fund is an **index fund**. An index is a list of securities, such as the 200 companies of the S&P/ASX 200. An index fund aims to match the index's performance, before fees and expenses, by holding the same securities in the same proportions. It does no stock picking, which is why it is called a **passive** fund.

Notice what the goal leaves out. Wikipedia says an index fund's objective is generally to keep its **tracking error**, how far it strays from its index, and its costs as low as possible, and it does not try to earn returns above the index by choosing securities. When the index falls, the fund falls with it, and the fees come off as well.

The case for index funds rests on cost. Wikipedia says an index fund is cheaper to run than an actively managed one, because the index is a known list, and it adds that turnover, the buying and selling inside a fund, has costs of its own that come off returns dollar for dollar. That is why the fee is worth reading before any promise of returns.

Many notable investors recommend index funds for their diversification, low fees and simplicity, and Wikipedia also reports a claim of historical outperformance over actively managed funds. Treat that last claim as those investors' view, since the article gives no figures with it and this lesson does not rely on it.

reveal.text: The same rule explains what an ETF is and what it can leave you exposed to, which is the next screen.

lead.text: An index fund can be sold in two forms. A managed fund pools money from many investors, with a manager buying and selling for the pool. An **exchange-traded fund**, or **ETF**, is a managed fund that trades on a stock exchange, so it is bought and sold like a share. In Australia most ETFs are passive and aim to track an index, although some are active, with a manager choosing investments to meet the fund's stated goal.
One ETF that tracks the S&P/ASX 200 gives you a share of Australia's 200 largest companies in a single trade, and Moneysmart notes that many ETFs have low management fees.

An ETF can also hold just one part of the market, such as technology, mining or financials, and a **sector ETF** like that is [[concentrated|A portfolio whose holdings can all be hurt by the same thing. Met earlier in this lesson.]] in the way Kyle was. Moneysmart lists sector risk and market risk among an ETF's risks, together with currency risk, and says that fees and trading costs also come off your return. Whether an ETF is diversified therefore depends on what it holds and on what its goal is.

reveal.text: A product can look like a spread and still concentrate the risk. What the holdings have in common tells you more than how many there are.

lead.text: A mix that suits you on the day you choose it will not stay that way. The holdings change in value by different amounts, so each one's share of the total moves, and Moneysmart calls this **drift**. Suppose a made-up mix starts as $60,000 of shares and $40,000 of bonds, which is 60% and 40%. If the shares then rise while the bonds fall, more of the portfolio ends up in shares, and the portfolio's overall risk is likely to rise with it.

Nobody chose that extra risk. **Rebalancing** is moving the mix back to the one that suits your goals, and Moneysmart names two ways: put new money, a tax refund for example, into the investment you want more of, or sell some of one investment and buy another. Selling may create a tax bill, so the first way has an advantage when you have the money to use it.

afterFigure.text: In the figure the shares have risen by 40% and the bonds have fallen by 10%. Nothing has been bought or sold, and the mix now carries a larger share in shares than the one that was chosen.

steps.headline: A made-up mix of $60,000 in shares and $40,000 in bonds sees its shares rise 40% and its bonds fall 10%. What mix has it drifted to, and what would put it back?

workedSteps.text: The shares are worth 40% more than before, so multiply $60,000 by 1.4.
The bonds are worth 10% less, so multiply $40,000 by 0.9.
The whole mix is now worth $120,000. Work out roughly what share of it is in shares.

To restore 60% in shares by selling, the shares must come down to 60% of the $120,000 and the difference goes into bonds. By adding money instead, only the bonds can grow, until the shares are 60% of the new total.

lessons.orientation: Say whether a portfolio is concentrated, which risks diversification does and does not remove, and what an index fund or ETF gives you and costs.
lessons.nextAction: Compare an investment property with a share fund on cash flow, costs, concentration and borrowing, and say what a property would have to do to cover a monthly shortfall.

blocks.text: Mia puts all $10,000 of her savings into the shares of one company. Ben puts $500 into each of twenty different companies. Both have bought shares and both hope they rise, yet they have taken on very different amounts of risk.
Wikipedia notes that one stock losing half its value in a year is not unusual, and the question below asks what that would mean for each of them.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say whether a portfolio is concentrated, which risks spreading removes and which it leaves, and what an index fund or ETF gives you and costs.
intro.whyItMatters: It tells you what a fund really protects you from and what it still leaves you exposed to.

recap.keyIdea: Spreading money across holdings that could fall for different reasons removes the risk of any one of them, the market's own risk stays, and an index fund or ETF is a low-cost way to hold the market but still has to be checked for what it holds.

blocks.text: You saw that five miners share one risk, so a count of holdings says little until you ask what could hurt them together. Most of the reduction in risk comes from the first few holdings, and fees can outweigh the gain from many more. Spreading across more shares in a market shrinks company risk and sector risk but leaves market risk, which is why an index fund still falls when its index does.

An index fund aims to match its index before fees, and an ETF is a fund traded like a share, so each of them is only as spread as what it holds. A mix of shares and bonds also drifts as prices move, and it needs rebalancing, by adding to the part that has fallen behind or by selling some of the part that has grown.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks these questions of one investment property bought with a loan: how much its rent covers, what it costs to hold, and what borrowing does to a loss.

lessons.title: Property against shares

lead.text: Moneysmart's table puts the rent coming in against four costs going out, and the last line is what the couple have to cover themselves. The costs are $2,725 for the loan, $225 for expenses, $216 for strata fees and $500 for repairs, which come to $3,666 a month. The rent is $2,250 of that, about 61%, so the **cash-flow shortfall** is $3,666 less $2,250, which is $1,416 a month.

A year of that is $1,416 times 12, or $16,992, and we'll round it to about $17,000. Moneysmart says Simon and Tiana can cover it from Tiana's salary and that they have an emergency fund for the stretches when no tenant is paying. The table has no tax line, and the 2026 Federal Budget, delivered on 12 May, announced changes to the tax rules for property investors that Moneysmart tells them to check with the ATO. The sources used here do not say what those changes are, so nothing in this lesson depends on them.

The first is the monthly table: rent of $2,250 against a loan repayment of $2,725 and $941 of other costs, leaving a monthly shortfall of $1,416. The second draws the costs and the rent as bars. The third gives the year's figures, with a shortfall of $16,992.

steps.headline: A $550,000 unit costs $16,992 a year more than it earns in rent. What yearly rise in its price would just match that?

workedSteps.text: The shortfall is a cash cost that the owners pay every year, while a price rise is a gain that they collect only when they sell. To compare the two, put them in the same units, by taking the yearly shortfall as a share of the price.
Judge roughly how big a yearly price rise that is. Round the shortfall to about $17,000 if that helps.

So the price would have to rise about 3.1% a year just to match the cash going out, and selling costs would come on top of that. The table does not say how much of the $2,725 repayment is interest and how much repays the loan, so treat 3.1% as a rough size for the hurdle.

lead.text: The monthly table shows what the unit costs while the couple own it, and there are costs at each end as well. Moneysmart lists stamp duty, conveyancing fees, legal costs and search fees when you buy, and Simon and Tiana's $23,000 of buying costs is about 4% of the price. When you sell there are the agent's fees, advertising costs and legal fees, and capital gains tax may apply. Moneysmart calls these **entry and exit costs** and describes them as high. In between come the ongoing costs: body corporate fees, property management fees, and repairs and maintenance.

Two more costs do not appear in a table of expected figures. **Vacancy** is one: when there is no tenant, you cover every cost yourself, which is why Moneysmart says not to rely on rent to cover the mortgage and why the couple keep an emergency fund. The other is time: Moneysmart notes that selling can take time, and a need for money means selling the whole property and paying the exit costs.

reveal.text: A property that does not cover its costs is paid for out of the owners' other income, and the rise in its price at the end has to make up the difference.

lead.text: A share fund can hold hundreds of companies. An investment property is one asset in one place, and Moneysmart's advice is to invest in more than property so your money is not all in one market, since putting everything in one market increases your risk and means the portfolio is not [[diversified|Spread across holdings that could fall for different reasons. Met in 'Diversification, index funds and ETFs'.]].

That is the concentration problem from the previous lesson in another form. The unit's value rests on one building in one place, a tenant leaving takes out all of the income at once, and a rise in interest rates can raise the repayments on a variable loan. Property does have its pull, since the unit earns rent and Moneysmart says it is often seen as less risky than other investments, although it warns of pitfalls like these.

Simon and Tiana borrowed $423,000 of a $550,000 purchase. Moneysmart calls borrowing to invest **gearing**, and its description is short: you get bigger returns when markets rise and larger losses when they fall, and you still have to repay the loan and the interest if the investment falls in value.

Moneysmart shows it with Kyle, whom we met in the last lesson. He has $10,000 of his own in shares and borrows another $15,000 to buy more, through what is called a margin loan, so his shares are worth $25,000. His lender will not let the loan go above 70% of the shares' value, and it measures that with the **loan to value ratio**, the loan divided by the value of the investments. Kyle starts at $15,000 out of $25,000, which is 60%. When commodity prices fall his shares lose $5,000, so they are worth $20,000 while the loan is still $15,000, and his ratio is 75%, over the limit.

The lender then makes a **margin call**, which usually gives him 24 hours to bring the ratio back down. Kyle put $2,000 of his savings towards the loan, cutting it to $13,000, which took the ratio to 65%.

diagram.alt: Three views of Kyle's shares as a bar split into his loan and his own money, with a dashed line at 70% of the shares' value. Before the fall the loan of $15,000 sits under the line at 60%. After a $5,000 fall the loan is above the line at 75%. After he repays $2,000 it is back under the line at 65%.

lead.text: Everything so far compares structure: how much of the costs the rent covers, what buying and selling cost, how concentrated the holding is and what borrowing does to a loss. The obvious question is which of the two has earned more, and the sources behind this lesson give no long-run returns for property or for shares, so there is no figure here to compare. A claim that one has beaten the other needs its own evidence.

The tax rules are the other gap. Moneysmart says the 2026 Federal Budget announced changes to how negative gearing and capital gains tax apply, and it sends readers to the ATO. The sources used here do not say what the changes are, so this lesson does not use them, and the after-tax cost of a property has to wait for current figures from the ATO.

reveal.text: When the figures you have cannot settle a claim, the useful reply is to ask where the claim's numbers come from.

lessons.orientation: Compare an investment property with a share fund on cash flow, costs, concentration and borrowing, and say what a property would have to do to cover a monthly shortfall.
lessons.nextAction: Match income protection, life, TPD and health cover to the risk each one covers, read the features that decide what a policy pays, and judge whether a hospital policy or the Medicare levy surcharge costs more.

blocks.text: Property is often seen as a less risky way to invest than shares, partly because a unit is easy to picture. Moneysmart agrees that it can seem more straightforward and then warns that there are pitfalls, and its example of a couple buying a unit shows one of them in dollars.

Simon and Tiana are looking at a $550,000 unit. They would pay $23,000 in buying costs, put in a deposit of $150,000 and borrow $423,000. Each month the rent is expected to be $2,250, and the costs are a loan repayment of $2,725, $225 for expenses, $216 in strata fees and $500 for repairs and maintenance.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read a property's cash flow, say what price rise it would need to cover a shortfall, and see what borrowing does to a loss.
intro.whyItMatters: A property can look safe and still cost more each month than it earns, and borrowing makes a fall in value a bigger share of your own money.

recap.keyIdea: A geared property can cost more each month than its rent earns, so its price has to rise to make up the gap, and borrowing turns a small fall in value into a large share of your own money.

blocks.text: Simon and Tiana's rent covers about 61% of a month's costs, which leaves $1,416 a month, about $17,000 a year, or a price rise of about 3.1% a year to match it before any selling cost. Entry and exit costs, vacancy and the difficulty of selling a part of a property add to the burden, and one property in one place is concentrated in a way that a fund of many holdings is not.

Kyle's loan stayed at $15,000 while his shares fell 20%, so he lost half of his own money, and a fall of about 14% was enough to bring a margin call. The sources used here give no long-run returns for property or for shares and do not describe the 2026 Budget's tax changes, so they say nothing about which has earned more.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns from growing money to protecting it, and starts from the risks that insurance covers and what each kind of cover pays.

lessons.title: Insurance

lead.text: Three risks account for most of what the covers in this lesson are for. The first is being unable to work for a while because of illness or injury, which leaves your bills running with no pay coming in. The second is dying while other people rely on your income or share your debts. The third is needing hospital care or other medical treatment.

Moneysmart pairs each risk with a cover. **Income protection** replaces part of your pay when illness or injury stops you working. **Life cover** pays a lump sum when you die. Health cover comes in three kinds, ambulance, hospital and extras, where extras means treatment outside hospital such as physiotherapy and dental. Moneysmart also names total and permanent disability cover, TPD, and trauma insurance as further cover for being sick or injured, and this lesson leaves both aside.

Income protection typically pays a share of your income before tax, such as 75% or 90%, calculated from your earnings over the twelve months before the illness or injury. Each policy has its own definition of disability. How much you receive depends on two settings. The **waiting period** is how long you must wait before payments start, and most policies offer between 14 days and two years. The **benefit period** is how long the payments last if you still cannot work, and most offer either two or five years, or payments until a set age such as 65.

Moneysmart also lists the type of premium, any minimum work hours and the exclusions among the features to compare. Premiums can be age-stepped, which means they are recalculated at each renewal, or set higher at the start and rising more slowly. In the figure the made-up policy has a 30 day wait and a two-year benefit period, and the three views show an illness of three weeks, six months and three years.

afterFigure.text: The same policy pays nothing for the first illness, pays for most of the second, and stops paying in the third while the person is still unable to work.

reveal.text: The last eleven months or so of Rav's three years are unpaid. A benefit period shorter than the illness leaves a gap at the end.

lead.text: Life cover pays a lump sum when you die, so that people who rely on your income can pay the mortgage, clear debts and meet everyday costs while they adjust. Moneysmart says it can help when a partner, children or other family depend on your income, or when you carry large debts or a mortgage. If nobody depends on you financially you may not need it, and Moneysmart suggests looking at income protection, TPD and trauma insurance in case you are sick or injured. Accidental death cover is different, since it pays only if you die in an accident.

How much cover is enough? Moneysmart's method is to find the **gap**: add up what your family would need, such as the mortgage, other debts, child care, school fees and living costs, take away what they would receive from super, savings, investments, leave and family support, and the difference is the amount to look for. A made-up family that would need $700,000 and would receive $250,000 has a gap of $450,000. Premiums generally rise as you get older.

reveal.text: Where a family's resources are larger than what it would need, there is no gap, and there is little for life cover to do.

lead.text: Income protection and life cover can be held inside super or outside it. Inside super the premiums are deducted from your balance, which Moneysmart says reduces your retirement savings, and outside super you pay them yourself. Cover that a fund sets up for its members without being asked is **default cover**, and it is paid for in the same way, out of the balance.

Because the premiums come out of the balance, default cover has a cost that never shows up as a bill, and over the years it reduces what is left for retirement. Whether it is worth keeping depends on what it would pay against what it costs, matched to the risks above. Whichever route you take, answer an insurer's questions honestly, because leaving out important details can lead the insurer to change or cancel the cover or to refuse a claim.

Private health insurance comes in three main kinds. Ambulance cover is for emergency transport. Hospital cover helps with the costs of a hospital stay. Extras cover, also called ancillary cover, is for treatment outside hospital, such as physiotherapy and dental. A combined policy has hospital and extras together, and holding private cover does not stop you being a public patient if you choose.

Three things shape what you pay and when you can claim. Premiums are **community rated**: Wikipedia says a fund cannot take your age, gender or pre-existing conditions into account when it works out the premium. Funds can impose waiting periods of their own, up to 12 months for a condition whose signs existed in the six months before you took out cover, 12 months for obstetric treatment and 2 months for everything else, so a new policy may not pay for treatment this month. And premiums change each year on 1 April, with an average rise of 4.41% in 2026.

A further rule rewards buying hospital cover early. **Lifetime Health Cover loading** adds 2% to the hospital part of the premium for each year of delay, so someone who first takes out hospital cover at 40 pays a loading of 20%, and it continues for 10 years. Basic hospital cover is enough to avoid it, and it does not apply to extras.

The Medicare levy is 2% of taxable income, and most Australians pay it. If you earn above a threshold and do not hold qualifying private hospital cover, you may also pay the **Medicare levy surcharge**, an extra 1%, 1.25% or 1.5% depending on your income. The ATO sets the tiers each year, and the table gives those for 2026-27 for a single person and for a family.

Two details do most of the work. The surcharge is worked out on the whole of your income for surcharge purposes, including the part below the threshold. The ATO's example is Tom, who is single, has no hospital cover, and has taxable income of $90,000 and $27,000 of reportable fringe benefits, which gives him $117,000 of income for surcharge purposes. That puts him in tier 1, and his surcharge for 2026-27 is 1% of $117,000, which is $1,170. The other detail is that only hospital cover counts, since Wikipedia says basic hospital cover satisfies the requirement and extras alone do not.

steps.headline: Cass has no hospital cover and income for surcharge purposes of $125,000 in 2026-27 (made up). What surcharge does she pay?

workedSteps.text: The single-person table puts $125,000 between $123,001 and $164,000, which is tier 2, and the rate for that tier is 1.25%.
The surcharge is charged on the whole of the income, so the rate is applied to all $125,000. Say roughly what she pays.
To see what the boundary does, compare an income of $123,000, the top of tier 1. Its surcharge is 1% of the whole, which is lower, and one more dollar of income lifts the surcharge by about $310.

lead.text: Is it cheaper to buy hospital cover or to pay the surcharge? Moneysmart says that for someone on a high income, buying the insurance may cost less than paying the surcharge, and the sums are simple enough to do. Suppose, with a made-up figure since the sources here give no current premiums, that a basic hospital policy costs $1,500 a year. The figure shows the surcharge at the edge of each tier for a single person with no hospital cover, and the policy's cost is the dashed line.

Throughout tier 1 the surcharge is at most $1,230, so it costs less than the policy. One dollar above $123,000 it jumps to about $1,540, and from there the policy costs less and also pays for hospital care, which the surcharge never does. The jumps at the boundaries are worth knowing, since one extra dollar of income costs about $1,050 at $105,000, about $310 at $123,000 and about $410 at $164,000.
Waiting too long to buy adds a cost of its own. At the same made-up $1,500 a year, a loading of 20% for someone who first buys hospital cover at 40 is $300 a year for 10 years, or $3,000 in all.

diagram.alt: Bars showing the Medicare levy surcharge for a single person at six incomes, with a dashed line for a made-up policy costing $1,500 a year. The surcharge is $0 at $105,000, about $1,050 at $105,001, $1,230 at $123,000, about $1,540 at $123,001, $2,050 at $164,000 and about $2,460 at $164,001. It jumps at each tier boundary and passes the policy's cost at $123,001.

lessons.orientation: Match income protection, life, TPD and health cover to the risk each one covers, read the features that decide what a policy pays, and judge whether a hospital policy or the Medicare levy surcharge costs more.
lessons.nextAction: Recognise the pressure, payment and trust-building patterns of investment and super scams in a message or advertisement, and read loss data to judge where the real losses are.

blocks.text: Insurance is something you pay for in the hope of never using it, which makes it easy to buy too much of the wrong cover and too little of the right one. A useful way to begin is to leave the products aside and list what could go wrong with your finances: you could be unable to work for a long time, you could die while other people depend on you, or you could need hospital care.
Each product is built for one of those risks, so for most people the question is which risks apply to them.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to match a cover to the risk it answers, read the settings that decide what income protection pays, and judge whether the Medicare levy surcharge costs more than a hospital policy.
intro.whyItMatters: A cover that does not match your risk is wasted money, and the surcharge rule changes what it costs to go without hospital cover.

recap.keyIdea: Each cover answers one risk: income protection pays part of your pay after a wait and for a limited time, life cover fills a family's gap, and the Medicare levy surcharge falls on the whole income once a threshold is passed, so it can cost more than a hospital policy.

blocks.text: You matched income protection to a person living on their pay, life cover to the gap a family would face, hospital cover to hospital stays and the surcharge rule, and extras to treatment outside hospital. Rav's policy paid for two of his three years, after a wait, because the waiting period and the benefit period set when payments start and stop. Cover inside super is paid for out of the balance.

The 2026-27 surcharge is a rate of 1%, 1.25% or 1.5% on the whole of the income for surcharge purposes, so a single extra dollar at a boundary can cost about $1,050, $310 or $410. Against a made-up $1,500 policy, the surcharge is the cheaper of the two through tier 1 and the dearer from $123,001, and the policy also pays for hospital care.

recap.nextHook: The last lesson looks at scams, and at how the patterns of an investment or super scam show up in a message, an advertisement or a phone call.

lessons.title: Scams

lead.text: The National Anti-Scam Centre's report on 2025 pulls together figures from five bodies: Scamwatch, ReportCyber, the Australian Financial Crimes Exchange, IDCARE and ASIC, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission. It says Australians reported losses of $2.18 billion, up 7.8% on 2024, from 481,523 reports, about 13,000 fewer than the 494,732 of 2024. **Investment scams**, which sell fake financial products, made up $837.7 million of that, about 38%, and the report calls them the most significant financial harm of any category. That was 11.4% less than the $945.0 million of 2024, so the category is shrinking and is still the largest.

The report also gives a median loss, the middle value, which means half of the losses are smaller. Scamwatch's median was $500 in 2024 and $400 in 2025, and the report reads the fall as more people being successfully targeted, for lower amounts.

diagram.alt: Two views of the National Anti-Scam Centre's 2025 figures drawn to scale. In the first, investment scam losses of $837.7 million are about 38% of the $2.18 billion total. In the second, investment scam losses fell 11.4% from $945.0 million in 2024 to $837.7 million in 2025.

lead.text: In an investment scam, Moneysmart says, the product does not exist and the person selling it is not who they claim to be. Some of the most sophisticated scams use AI to build a whole footprint around the offer, with fake advertisements, reviews, news articles and celebrity endorsements, so the offer looks supported from every side.

The figure follows the path Moneysmart describes. A person may follow an advertisement on a familiar platform to a fake news article with celebrity endorsements and made-up comments. Once they give their details, the scammers follow up with scripted phone calls, a fake investment platform and small profit payments, all of which are there to build **trust**. The money itself ends up with overseas criminals, and Moneysmart says it is very unlikely to be recovered.

afterFigure.text: The small payments are the part that surprises people, since they look like proof. Moneysmart treats them as part of the script that builds trust, and they say nothing about whether the platform is real.

diagram.alt: Five boxes in a row showing the path of an AI-assisted investment scam as Moneysmart describes it: an advertisement on a well-known platform, a fake news article with celebrity endorsements, the victim giving their details, scripted calls and a fake investment platform, and small profit payments that build trust. Each view highlights one step.

reveal.text: A payment like that is there to make the next request feel safe. It tells you what the scammer wants you to believe and nothing about the platform.

lead.text: Moneysmart lists signs that an investment offer may be a scam. The person has no Australian financial services licence, or says that none is needed. They contact you constantly and press you to decide quickly. They borrow the name of a reputable organisation to look credible, or they hold a prospectus that is not registered with ASIC, or they offer very high returns. Offers of big returns with almost no risk, guaranteed profits, exclusive access and insider tips belong on the same list, because Moneysmart's point is that a legitimate investment always carries some risk.

The check is as concrete as the signs. Moneysmart says to use a licensed Australian financial services provider and to confirm that they appear on the financial firm directory of AFCA, the Australian Financial Complaints Authority. The National Anti-Scam Centre's routine is **Stop, Check, Protect**: do not give money or personal information if you are unsure, check who you are dealing with and whether the message or call could be fake, and act quickly if something feels wrong. Be suspicious if you are asked to pay with gift cards or cryptocurrency, and do not click links in a suspicious text message.
Scammers use professional websites, advertisements, fake reviews and celebrity endorsements, so none of these shows that an offer is genuine.

reveal.text: Checking has to use sources that the offer does not control, such as the AFCA directory and ASIC.

lead.text: How the money moves tells you a good deal, and the report gives figures. Cryptocurrency and digital currency exchanges were the payment method with the highest overall losses in 2025, at $121.3 million, which was 36.2% of overall losses, and the report describes this as a big change from 2024, when bank transfers led. Bank transfers are still the method that scammers request most often, and they led to losses of $118.1 million from 8,858 reports.

That is why Moneysmart tells you to be suspicious when you are asked to pay with gift cards or cryptocurrency. It also explains why recovery is hard, since many investment scams involve overseas criminal networks, and scammers often shuffle the money rapidly from account to account, or change it into cryptocurrency, which makes it harder to trace. The last step of Stop, Check, Protect is to act quickly if something feels wrong.

reveal.text: The best protection comes before the payment, which is why the check comes before the money.

lead.text: A count of reports is not a count of losses, and the report gives a clear case. In 2025 email was the contact method that people reported most often, with 84,861 reports, yet only 4,329 of the people reporting lost money, which the report gives as 5.0%, or about 5%. Roughly 95 in every 100 email reports involved no reported loss.

Phone calls look quite different. Reports with loss numbered 2,012 in 2025, down from 2,179, and losses totalled $72.5 million, which is 32.0% less than in 2024. Even so, Scamwatch data points to larger individual losses from phone scams, with a median of $3,800 against $400 for scams reported to Scamwatch overall. A count of reports says how often a method is reported and nothing about how much people lose when it works.

reveal.text: To compare methods fairly you need the money lost and the number who lost it, and a count of reports gives neither.

lead.text: The report says that none of a person's education, status, wealth, work, age, health or culture gives them immunity from scams, and that the right circumstances can catch anybody. Losses are not shared equally, though. The report cites the Australian Bureau of Statistics for older Australians making up about 17.1% of the population, and they account for 26.5% of the losses reported to Scamwatch, which is about one and a half times their share. It adds that the median loss is higher for First Nations communities and for culturally and linguistically diverse communities.

The same patterns turn up in scams aimed at your super. The ATO says that taking super out before a condition of release is met is illegal, and it warns about people who promote early-access schemes. The usual version tells you to set up a self-managed super fund, or SMSF, so that you can take your super out and spend it on things like clearing a credit card, buying a house or car, or going on a holiday.

If someone approaches you with such an offer, the ATO says to check that they are a licensed financial adviser, which you can do on ASIC's Moneysmart website. Until you have checked, the Stop, Check, Protect routine applies: give no money or personal information. Joining an illegal scheme costs far more than the super you take out: the amount is included as income in your tax return, which can bring additional income tax, tax shortfall penalties and interest.

reveal.text: Pressure to sign today and a promise of early access are each a warning sign. Together they are a reason to stop and check.

lessons.orientation: Recognise the pressure, payment and trust-building patterns of investment and super scams in a message or advertisement, and read loss data to judge where the real losses are.
lessons.nextAction: You can now read an investment or super offer for its warning signs, and check the provider before you pay.

blocks.text: The National Anti-Scam Centre's report on 2025 says Australians reported losses of $2.18 billion to scams that year, 7.8% more than in 2024, although the number of reports fell a little to 481,523. The largest single category was scams that sell fake investments, with $837.7 million of the loss.

Those scams copy the shape of a real investment, with a product, a promised return and a provider you are meant to rely on. What gives them away is what a real investment would not do, such as guarantee a return, press you to decide quickly or ask to be paid in gift cards.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to recognise the pressure, payment and trust-building patterns of an investment or super scam, and read loss data to judge where the real losses are.
intro.whyItMatters: A scam can look like any other investment offer, and the few checks in this lesson work whatever the offer looks like.

recap.keyIdea: An investment scam builds belief step by step and shows itself through pressure, guarantees and unusual payment methods, so the defence is to stop and check the provider yourself, and the most reported contact method is not the costliest.

blocks.text: Investment scams were $837.7 million of the $2.18 billion reported lost in 2025. They run from an advertisement and a fake news article to scripted calls, a fake platform and small profit payments, and the payments build trust without showing that the platform is real. Moneysmart's red flags are a missing licence, constant pressure, a borrowed name, an unregistered prospectus and very high returns, and its routine, with the National Anti-Scam Centre, is Stop, Check, Protect.

Email was the most reported contact method yet only about 5% of those reporters lost money, while phone scams had a median loss of $3,800. Nobody is immune, and the ATO's warning applies to super: a promise of early access through an SMSF is an illegal scheme that costs more than it releases.

questions.prompt: In an invented table, nothing is taxed up to $20,000 and income over $20,000 is taxed at 10c for each $1 over. Zoe's taxable income is $30,000. How much tax does she pay?
